revision_note: v1 ran 3,176 chars and enumerated 7.42(b) and 7.46(a) in full; trimmed to the classification scheme, the three strategy elements and the notification duty, which is what the question asks
ideal_answer:
Recall classification. FDA assigns a Class I, II or III designation reflecting the relative health hazard (21 CFR 7.3(m)): Class I where there is a reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II where consequences may be temporary or medically reversible, or serious consequences are remote; Class III where adverse consequences are not likely. The classification follows a health hazard evaluation by an ad hoc committee of FDA scientists (7.41(a), (b)).

Recall strategy. Developed by FDA for an agency-requested recall and by the firm for a firm-initiated one (7.42(a)(1)), addressing three elements (7.42(b)): depth of recall - consumer/user, retail or wholesale level; public warning, reserved for urgent situations where other means are inadequate; and effectiveness checks, at Level A (100% of consignees) through Level E (none).

Firm-initiated recall. A firm may act of its own volition; where it believes the product violative it is requested to notify its FDA district office immediately with the product identity, the reason and circumstances of discovery, a risk evaluation, quantities produced and in distribution, distribution information, its recall communication and proposed strategy (7.46(a)). FDA then assigns the classification and lists the recall in the weekly Enforcement Report.

revision_note: v1 ran 1,886 chars listing all eleven controls as a block; condensed while keeping every control, because the question asks what controls are required and omitting any would reintroduce the incompleteness this example targets
ideal_answer: Persons using closed systems to create, modify, maintain or transmit electronic records must employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity and, when appropriate, the confidentiality of those records, and to ensure the signer cannot readily repudiate the signed record (21 CFR 11.10). The required controls are: (a) validation of systems, including the ability to discern invalid or altered records; (b) the ability to generate accurate and complete copies in human readable and electronic form for agency inspection; (c) protection of records for accurate and ready retrieval throughout the retention period; (d) limiting system access to authorized individuals; (e) secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that do not obscure previously recorded information; (f) operational system checks enforcing permitted sequencing; (g) authority checks; (h) device checks on the source of data input; (i) determination that personnel have the education, training and experience for their tasks; (j) written policies holding individuals accountable for actions under their electronic signatures; and (k) controls over systems documentation, covering its distribution, access and use and revision and change control.

revision_note: v1 ran 3,510 chars reproducing all ten paragraphs of 111.15; condensed to the six areas the key elements name
ideal_answer:
21 CFR 111.15 requires the physical plant and grounds to be kept so as to protect against contamination of components, dietary supplements and contact surfaces.

Grounds (111.15(a)): store equipment properly, remove litter and waste and cut weeds or grass so as not to attract, harbor or breed pests; maintain roads, yards and parking lots; drain areas that could contaminate by seepage or filth; operate waste treatment and disposal adequately; and where bordering grounds outside your control are not so maintained, exclude pests, dirt and filth by inspection or extermination.

Plant (111.15(b)): maintain it clean, sanitary and in sufficient repair.

Cleaning and sanitizing agents (111.15(c)): use agents free from microorganisms of public health significance that are safe and adequate in use; hold toxic materials only where necessary for sanitation, laboratory testing, plant or equipment operation, or plant operations, and identify and hold them so as to protect against contamination.

Pest control (111.15(d)): allow no animals or pests, except guard or guide dogs in some areas; take effective exclusion measures; and use pesticides only with precautions against contamination.

Plumbing (111.15(f)) must carry sufficient water, convey sewage and liquid waste, avoid being a source of contamination, provide floor drainage, and prevent backflow or cross connection with potable supplies. Bathrooms must be adequate, readily accessible and kept clean (111.15(h)).

revision_note: v1 ran 4,216 chars, the longest in the set, reproducing 117.20(b)(1)-(7) and 117.35(a)-(f) in full; condensed to the five areas the key elements name
ideal_answer:
Two sections of subpart B apply.

Plant and grounds (21 CFR 117.20). Grounds under the operator's control must be kept so as to protect against contamination of food: store equipment properly, remove litter and waste, cut weeds or grass that may attract, breed or harbor pests; maintain roads, yards and parking lots; drain areas that may contribute contamination by seepage or foot-borne filth; operate waste treatment adequately; and where bordering grounds outside the operator's control are not so maintained, exclude pests, dirt and filth by inspection or extermination (117.20(a)). The plant must be suitable in size, construction and design to facilitate maintenance and sanitary operations, with adequate space, precautions against allergen cross-contact and contamination, protection for outdoor bulk vessels, cleanable floors, walls and ceilings, adequate lighting with glass protection, adequate ventilation, and screening against pests (117.20(b)).

Sanitary operations (117.35). Buildings, fixtures and facilities must be kept clean, sanitary and in adequate repair (117.35(a)). Cleaning compounds and sanitizing agents must be free from undesirable microorganisms and safe and adequate in use, and toxic materials identified, held and stored so as to protect against contamination (117.35(b)). Pests must not be allowed in any area, save guard, guide or pest-detecting dogs where contamination is unlikely (117.35(c)). Food-contact surfaces must be cleaned as frequently as necessary against allergen cross-contact and contamination, and non-food-contact surfaces as necessary (117.35(d), (e)).

revision_note: v1 ran 3,979 chars and enumerated all nineteen SOP items of 606.100(b); condensed to the four areas the key elements name, and cites only sections present in the packed evidence
ideal_answer:
Personnel (21 CFR 606.20). Personnel responsible for the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage or distribution of blood or blood components must be adequate in number, educational background, training and experience, including professional training as necessary (606.20(b)), and persons whose presence can adversely affect the safety and purity of the products must be excluded from those areas (606.20(c)).

Standard operating procedures (606.100). Establishments must establish, maintain and follow written SOPs for all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage and distribution of blood and blood components for allogeneic and autologous transfusion and further manufacturing (606.100(b)). The enumerated procedures run from donor eligibility criteria and donor qualifying tests through component preparation, in-process and repeat testing, pretransfusion testing, investigation of adverse donor and recipient reactions, storage temperatures, expiration dating, reissue criteria, quality control of supplies and reagents, equipment maintenance and calibration, and labeling safeguards.

Records (606.160). Records must be maintained concurrently with each significant step so that all steps can be clearly traced, and must be legible, indelible and identify the person performing the work (606.160(a)(1)).

Retention (606.160(d)). Records must be retained beyond the expiration date as necessary to facilitate reporting of unfavourable clinical reactions, and individual product records for no less than 10 years after processing records are completed, or 6 months after the latest expiration date, whichever is later.

revision_note: v1 ran 3,771 chars and reproduced the whole 207.49(a) listing-content enumeration; condensed to NDC composition, labeler-code assignment and the listing duty, which is what the question asks
ideal_answer:
The NDC (21 CFR 207.33). Each finished drug product or unfinished drug subject to listing must have a unique NDC identifying its labeler, product and package size and type (207.33(a)). It is a 10- or 11-digit numeric code in three segments: a labeler code of 4, 5 or 6 digits, assigned by FDA; a product code of 3 or 4 digits; and a package code of 1 or 2 digits identifying package size and type (207.33(b)). Permissible configurations are 5-4-1, 6-4-1, 5-3-2, 6-3-2 or, for a 4-digit labeler code, only 4-4-2, and a given labeler code may use only one product-package configuration.

Assignment. Anyone manufacturing, repacking, relabeling or private label distributing a drug subject to listing must obtain a labeler code (207.33(c)). An NDC is proposed for assignment when first submitted with listing information, and FDA assigns it on receiving that information provided the code conforms and is not reserved for or already assigned to another drug (207.33(d)).

Listing (207.41). Each registrant must list every drug it manufactures, repacks, relabels or salvages for commercial distribution, and a domestic registrant must do so whether or not the drug enters interstate commerce (207.41(a)). Listing information is submitted under 207.49, 207.53 and 207.54 according to the activities performed (207.41(b)).

revision_note: v1 ran 3,680 chars and reproduced the contents of 1003.20, 1003.21 and all three plan sections; condensed to the two duties the question asks about, citing only sections in the packed evidence
ideal_answer:
Two duties follow.

Notification (21 CFR 1003.10). A manufacturer who discovers that an electronic product it produced, assembled or imported, and which has left its place of manufacture, has a defect or fails to comply with an applicable Federal standard must immediately notify the Secretary under 1003.20 (1003.10(a)), and, except as authorised by 1003.30, must notify with reasonable promptness the dealers or distributors to whom the product was delivered and the purchaser and any subsequent transferee, where known or identifiable on reasonable inquiry (1003.10(b)). The notice to the Secretary must be confirmed in writing and identify the product, the numbers produced and distributed, the defect or non-compliance, an evaluation of the related hazards, the measures to be taken, and the date and circumstances of discovery (1003.20).

Remedy (1004.1). Where notification under 1003.10(b) is required, the manufacturer must either bring the product into conformity or remedy the defect without charge, reimbursing transportation expenses; or replace it with a like or equivalent product complying with each applicable Federal standard and free of safety-related defect; or refund the cost to the purchaser (1004.1(a)). The action must be taken under a plan approved by the Secretary (1004.1(b)).

revision_note: v1 ran 2,779 chars and enumerated the 4.4(b)(2) and (b)(3) additions in full; condensed to the structure of the election, citing only sections in the packed evidence
ideal_answer:
For a single-entity or co-packaged combination product, compliance with all applicable CGMP requirements must be achieved through a CGMP operating system that satisfies either the specifics of each set of CGMP regulations listed in 21 CFR 4.3 as they apply to each constituent part, or the alternative in 4.4(b) (4.4(a)). The second is the streamlined approach: demonstrate compliance with one regime in full, then add a defined list of provisions from the other.

Where the operating system has been shown to comply with the drug CGMP requirements, or the medical gas requirements as applicable, the product must additionally satisfy specified ISO 13485 clauses and Part 820 provisions covering general requirements and management responsibility, design and development with documented risk management, purchasing, analysis of data and complaint handling, installation and servicing (4.4(b)(1)).

Where instead the system has been shown to comply with the device QMSR requirements, specified drug CGMP provisions must also be met, including testing and approval of components, containers and closures, calculation of yield, tamper-evident packaging for OTC products, expiration dating, testing and release for distribution, stability and special testing, and reserve samples (4.4(b)(2)).

So it is a choice of base regime plus a closed list of additions - not a free blend, and not an exemption from either.

revision_note: v1 ran 1,398 chars and discussed the neighbouring component and blood carve-outs, which are not key elements; dropping them let 820.1(b), the conflict rule the question turns on, into the packed evidence within the production budget
ideal_answer:
Yes. The provisions of Part 820 apply to manufacturers of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps) that are devices - that is, devices subject to premarket review or notification, or exempt from notification (21 CFR 820.1(a)(4)).

What else applies: such HCT/Ps remain subject to Part 1271, so both sets of requirements are engaged.

How they interact: the QMSR supplements the regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise, and to the extent a requirement in Part 820 conflicts with a requirement elsewhere, the regulation specifically applicable to the device in question supersedes the more general one (820.1(b)). So where Part 1271 speaks specifically to an HCT/P, it governs over the more general Part 820 provision.

revision_note: v1 ran 1,944 chars; condensed and the 1271.3 reference removed, since that section is not in the packed evidence and the carve-out can be stated without it
ideal_answer:
Part 820 is the quality management system regulation (QMSR), setting the CGMP requirements for devices. Its requirements govern the methods used in, and the facilities and controls used for, the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use (21 CFR 820.1(a)).

Who is subject. Any manufacturer engaged in any of those activities for a finished device must establish and maintain a quality management system appropriate for its specific device(s), and must document a quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, and the other applicable requirements of the part (820.1(a); 820.10(a)). Those subject include, but are not limited to, manufacturers performing contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking or specification development, and initial distributors of foreign entities performing those functions. A manufacturer engaged in only some of the operations subject to the part need only comply with the requirements applicable to those operations (820.1(a)).

Carve-outs. The part does not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, though they are encouraged to consider its provisions (820.1(a)(2)), nor to manufacturers of blood and blood components for transfusion or further manufacturing, who are subject to subchapter F (820.1(a)(3)).

revision_note: v1 ran 2,701 chars and quoted 600.11(a)-(f) in detail, which could not be packed alongside 600.10 and 210.2 within the production budget; condensed to the four standards areas and the Part 211 interaction
ideal_answer:
Part 600, subpart B sets general standards in four areas.

Personnel (21 CFR 600.10(b), (c)). Personnel must have capabilities commensurate with their assigned functions, a thorough understanding of the operations they perform, and the necessary training and experience for individual products; persons whose presence can adversely affect a product's safety and purity must be excluded from the room where manufacture is in progress, and personnel performing sterile operations must wear clean or sterilized protective clothing.

Physical establishment, equipment, animals and care (600.11). Rooms and work areas where products are manufactured or stored must be kept orderly, clean and free of dirt, dust, vermin and objects not required for manufacturing, with precautions against drainage clogging and back-siphonage and against extraneous infectious agents.

Interaction with Part 211. The drug CGMP regulations and the Part 600 through 680 requirements supplement, and do not supersede, each other unless the regulations explicitly provide otherwise; in the event of a conflict, the regulation specifically applicable to the drug product in question supersedes the more general (21 CFR 210.2(a)). A biological product manufacturer must therefore satisfy both, with the more specific provision controlling.

revision_note: v1 ran 3,391 chars and reproduced the guidance's enforcement-discretion passages at length; condensed to which provisions apply and what the guidance does and does not change
ideal_answer:
Which provisions apply. Part 11 reaches a cloud-hosted LIMS through the records it holds: it applies to records in electronic form created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirement in agency regulations (21 CFR 11.1(b)). Whether 11.10 or 11.30 governs turns on whether the system is closed or open. A closed system attracts the full set of 11.10 controls - validation, accurate and complete copies, record protection, access limits, audit trails, operational, authority and device checks, training, written accountability policies and documentation controls. For an open system, 11.30 applies: the persons responsible for the record content must ensure authenticity, integrity and, as appropriate, confidentiality from creation to receipt, including the 11.10 controls as appropriate plus additional measures such as document encryption and appropriate digital signature standards. The obligations fall on the regulated person, not the host; where the vendor controls access the arrangement is likely an open system.

Effect of the guidance. FDA's "Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application" (final, 2003-09-05, Docket FDA-2003-D-0143) states that FDA will narrowly interpret part 11's scope and intends to exercise enforcement discretion over the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements. It does not remove anything: records must still be maintained or submitted in accordance with the underlying predicate rules, and the guidance is non-binding - it represents FDA's current thinking.

revision_note: v1 ran 3,192 chars and listed all nine functions of 111.105; condensed to the independence rule and the character of the QC role, which is the distinction asked for
ideal_answer:
The difference is one of function and independence.

Separation of duties (21 CFR 111.12(b)). You must identify who is responsible for quality control operations. Each person identified to perform them must be qualified and must have responsibilities related to performing those operations that are distinct and separate from the responsibilities that person has when not performing them. That is the source of the independence: a person may hold both kinds of duty, but the quality control duties must be distinct, so production work is not approved by the same person acting in the same capacity. Both groups share the same baseline - each person engaged in manufacturing, packaging, labeling or holding, or in quality control operations, must have the education, training or experience to perform the assigned functions (111.12(c)).

Quality control functions (111.105). Quality control personnel must ensure that operations ensure the quality of the dietary supplement and that it is packaged and labeled as specified in the master manufacturing record. Their role is approval and review, not production: approving or rejecting all processes, specifications, written procedures, controls, tests and examinations and any deviations from them that may affect identity, purity, strength or composition; reviewing and approving supplier qualification documentation; ensuring representative and reserve samples are collected and held; and determining whether all specifications established under 111.70(a) are met.

So production personnel carry out the work; quality control personnel approve the processes governing it and judge whether specifications are met, under duties that must be separate from any production role they hold.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,938 chars and covered all six categories in 117.135(c); condensed to the three the question asks about, keeping the shared frame and the overlap point
ideal_answer:
All three are kinds of preventive control under 21 CFR 117.135(c) and share the same frame: you must identify and implement preventive controls giving assurances that hazards requiring a preventive control will be significantly minimized or prevented and the food will not be adulterated under section 402 of the Act (117.135(a)(1)); they include controls at critical control points, if any, and controls other than at CCPs that are appropriate for food safety (117.135(a)(2)); and they must be written (117.135(b)). What differs is what each controls.

Process controls (117.135(c)(1)) are procedures, practices and processes ensuring control of parameters during operations such as heat processing, acidifying, irradiating and refrigerating, and must include the parameters associated with control of the hazard and the maximum or minimum values to which any biological, chemical or physical parameter must be controlled. They are characterised by measurable limits.

Food allergen controls (117.135(c)(2)) control food allergens and must include the procedures employed for protecting food from allergen cross-contact, including during storage, handling and use, and for labeling the finished food so it is not misbranded under section 403(w).

Sanitation controls (117.135(c)(3)) ensure the facility is kept in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens, biological hazards from employee handling and food allergen hazards, and must include the cleanliness of food-contact surfaces and the prevention of allergen cross-contact and cross-contamination.

Note the deliberate overlap: allergen cross-contact is addressed by both (c)(2)(i) and (c)(3)(ii).

revision_note: v1 ran 2,878 chars and reproduced the serious-injury and malfunction definitions in full plus 803.50(a); condensed to the definitions and the operative difference
ideal_answer:
Both are MDR reportable events for a manufacturer and both carry the same 30-calendar-day deadline; the trigger differs, and the malfunction limb adds a test the serious-injury limb does not.

Definitions (21 CFR 803.3). Serious injury means an injury or illness that is life-threatening, results in permanent impairment of a body function or permanent damage to a body structure, or necessitates medical or surgical intervention to preclude such permanent impairment or damage (803.3(w)). Malfunction means the failure of a device to meet its performance specifications or otherwise perform as intended, performance specifications including all claims made in the labeling (803.3(k)).

The duty (803.50(a)). A manufacturer must report no later than 30 calendar days after becoming aware of information from any source reasonably suggesting that a device it markets may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury (803.50(a)(1)), or has malfunctioned and that this or a similar device it markets would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if the malfunction were to recur (803.50(a)(2)).

The operative difference. A serious-injury report turns on what happened, assessed against the 803.3(w) criteria. A malfunction report turns on a failure to perform as intended plus a forward-looking recurrence test: the question is not whether anyone was hurt but whether recurrence would likely cause death or serious injury. So a malfunction that harmed nobody is still reportable if that test is met, and one that cannot meet it is not reportable on that limb.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,806 chars and reproduced 117.160 and 117.165 in detail; condensed to the five verification activities and the substance of validation and effectiveness verification
ideal_answer:
Verification activities must include, as appropriate to the nature of the preventive control and its role in the facility's food safety system, five things (21 CFR 117.155(a)): validation in accordance with 117.160; verification that monitoring is being conducted as required by 117.140; verification that appropriate decisions about corrective actions are being made as required by 117.140; verification of implementation and effectiveness in accordance with 117.165; and reanalysis in accordance with 117.170. All verification activities must be documented in records (117.155(b)).

Validation (117.160) must establish that the preventive controls are adequate to control the hazard. It must be performed or overseen by a preventive controls qualified individual before implementation of the food safety plan, or within 90 calendar days after production first begins where necessary to demonstrate the controls can be implemented as designed, and again on a change to a control measure or where a reanalysis reveals the need (117.160(b)(1)); and it must include obtaining and evaluating scientific and technical evidence (117.160(b)(2)). Validation is not required for food allergen controls, sanitation controls, the recall plan or the supply-chain program (117.160(c)).

Verification of implementation and effectiveness (117.165(a)) requires calibration of process monitoring and verification instruments, product testing, environmental monitoring where contamination of a ready-to-eat food with an environmental pathogen is a hazard requiring a preventive control, and review of monitoring and corrective action records.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,733 chars and reproduced 117.150(b) in full; condensed to the corrective-action steps, the corrections distinction and the records duty
ideal_answer:
A metal detector failing mid-shift is a preventive control that has not been properly implemented, so 21 CFR 117.150 governs.

Corrective action (117.150(a)). Except as provided by 117.150(c), you must have established and implemented written corrective action procedures to be taken if preventive controls are not properly implemented. They must describe the steps to ensure that appropriate action is taken to identify and correct the problem; that appropriate action is taken, when necessary, to reduce the likelihood of recurrence; that all affected food is evaluated for safety; and that all affected food is prevented from entering commerce if you cannot ensure it is not adulterated under section 402 or misbranded under section 403(w) (117.150(a)(2)). So: correct the failure, address recurrence, evaluate the food produced while the detector was down, and hold it unless you can establish it is not adulterated.

Corrections, and the distinction (117.150(c)). You need not comply with 117.150(a) or (b) where you act in a timely manner to identify and correct conditions inconsistent with the food allergen controls in 117.135(c)(2)(i) or the sanitation controls in 117.135(c)(3)(i) or (ii), or to correct a minor and isolated problem that does not directly impact product safety. A metal detector failure is a process control failure affecting product safety, so it is a corrective action, not a correction.

Records (117.150(d)). All corrective actions, and when appropriate corrections, must be documented.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,657 chars and reproduced the low-acid canned food and research-use carve-outs; condensed to who is bound and the non-duplication provisions in both directions
ideal_answer:
They bind different persons and are drafted not to duplicate each other.

Who is bound. The Part 117 supply-chain program binds the receiving facility: except as provided in 21 CFR 117.405(a)(2) and (3), the receiving facility must establish and implement a risk-based supply-chain program for those raw materials and other ingredients for which it has identified a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control (117.405(a)(1)), and the program must be written (117.405(b)). FSVP binds the importer: for each food you import you must develop, maintain and follow a foreign supplier verification program giving adequate assurances that your foreign supplier produces the food in compliance with processes and procedures providing the same level of public health protection as the applicable requirements (1.502(a)).

Non-duplication, in both directions. A receiving facility that is an importer, is in compliance with the FSVP requirements of part 1 subpart L, and holds documentation of verification activities under 1.506(e), need not conduct supplier verification activities for that raw material or ingredient (117.405(a)(2)). Conversely, an importer that is a receiving facility subject to section 418 of the Act is deemed in compliance with subpart L - except for 1.509 - if it implements preventive controls under 117.135, is not required to implement one, or has established a risk-based supply-chain program under subpart G of part 117 (1.502(c)).

The Part 117 requirements also do not apply to food supplied for research or evaluation use meeting the conditions in 117.405(a)(3).

revision_note: v1 ran 2,622 chars and reproduced 803.18(b) and (d) in full; condensed to the procedure contents, the file contents and the retention periods
ideal_answer:
Written procedures (21 CFR 803.17). A user facility, importer or manufacturer must develop, maintain and implement written MDR procedures covering internal systems providing for timely and effective identification, communication and evaluation of events that may be subject to MDR requirements; a standardized review process for determining when an event meets the reporting criteria; and timely transmission of complete medical device reports to manufacturers or to FDA (803.17(a)). They must also cover documentation and recordkeeping for the information evaluated to determine reportability, the reports and information submitted, information evaluated in preparing annual reports, and systems ensuring access to information for timely follow-up and inspection (803.17(b)).

MDR event files (803.18). These must be established, clearly identified and maintained to facilitate timely access (803.18(a)). They must hold information or references relating to the adverse event, including all documentation of the deliberations and decision-making used to decide whether a device-related death, serious injury or malfunction was reportable; copies of all reports submitted; and copies of FDA's electronic acknowledgments (803.18(b)(1)).

Retention (803.18(c)). A user facility must retain an MDR event file for 2 years from the date of the event. A manufacturer or importer must retain it for 2 years from the date of the event or for a period equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,591 chars; condensed the Part 211 half and kept the explicit statement that the Barr framework cannot be sourced from the supplied evidence
ideal_answer:
What Part 211 requires. An out-of-specification HPLC result is a failure of a batch or a component to meet a specification, and 21 CFR 211.192 requires that any unexplained discrepancy or such a failure be thoroughly investigated, whether or not the batch has already been distributed. The investigation must extend to other batches of the same drug product and other drug products that may have been associated with the specific failure or discrepancy, and a written record of it must be made including the conclusions and follow-up. All production and control records must in any event be reviewed and approved by the quality control unit before a batch is released or distributed (211.192).

The control framework the result sits in. Laboratory controls must include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans and test procedures (211.160(b)), and any change to them must be drafted by the appropriate organisational unit and reviewed and approved by the quality control unit (211.160(a)). So the result may not simply be set aside.

On the Barr decision framework, I cannot set it out from the evidence supplied. The two-phase structure - a Phase I laboratory investigation, then a Phase II full-scale investigation where no laboratory root cause is found - and the principle that a result may not be invalidated without an assignable cause come from case law and guidance, not from the text of Part 211, and neither is in the evidence I have.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,420 chars and reproduced 807.20(a)(1)-(6) and 830.20(a)-(c); condensed to which part does what and the two Part 820 hooks
ideal_answer:
Three parts, each doing a different job, with Part 820 providing the quality-system hooks.

Registration and listing - Part 807. An owner or operator of an establishment not exempt under section 510(g) of the Act or subpart D of Part 807, engaged in the manufacture, preparation, propagation, compounding, assembly or processing of a device intended for human use, must register and submit a device list (21 CFR 807.20(a)). The duty expressly reaches specification developers, those who sterilize or otherwise make a device for another, repackagers and relabelers, reprocessors of single-use devices, and initial importers.

Unique device identification - Part 830. A UDI must be issued under a system operated by FDA or an FDA-accredited issuing agency and must conform to the incorporated ISO/IEC standards (830.20).

How Part 820 interacts. Part 820 sets neither the registration, listing nor UDI requirements; it requires the quality management system to reach them. For Clause 7.5.8 in ISO 13485, Identification, the manufacturer must document a system to assign unique device identification in accordance with the requirements of part 830 (820.10(b)(1)). On the records side, the UDI must be recorded for each medical device or batch of devices (820.35(c)).

So Part 807 is the registration and listing regime, Part 830 sets what a UDI must be, and Part 820 requires the assignment system and the record.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,206 chars and listed all nine cleanliness methods; condensed while keeping the six areas the key elements name
ideal_answer:
Under 21 CFR 117.10 the management of the establishment must take reasonable measures and precautions to ensure the following.

Disease control (117.10(a)). Any person shown by medical examination or supervisory observation to have, or appearing to have, an illness, open lesion including boils, sores or infected wounds, or any other abnormal source of microbial contamination presenting a reasonable possibility of contamination must be excluded from operations that may be expected to result in such contamination until the condition is corrected.

Cleanliness (117.10(b)). All persons working in direct contact with food, food-contact surfaces and food-packaging materials must conform to hygienic practices while on duty to the extent necessary to protect against allergen cross-contact and contamination. The methods include wearing suitable outer garments; maintaining adequate personal cleanliness; washing hands thoroughly, and sanitizing if necessary, in an adequate hand-washing facility before starting work, after each absence from the work station and whenever the hands may have become soiled; removing unsecured jewelry and hand jewelry that cannot be sanitized, or covering it; keeping gloves used in food handling intact, clean and sanitary; wearing hair nets, headbands, caps, beard covers or other effective hair restraints where appropriate; storing personal belongings away from exposed food; and confining eating, gum, beverages and tobacco to other areas.

revision_note: v1 ran 2,184 chars and listed all eight PCQI duties plus the qualified-auditor role; condensed to the definition, the duties and the training record
ideal_answer:
Who the person is. A preventive controls qualified individual is a qualified individual who has successfully completed training in the development and application of risk-based preventive controls at least equivalent to that received under a standardized curriculum recognized as adequate by FDA, or is otherwise qualified through job experience to develop and apply a food safety system (21 CFR 117.3; 117.180(c)(1)). Job experience may qualify the individual where it has provided knowledge at least equivalent to the standardized curriculum. All applicable training must be documented in records including the date and type of training and the persons trained (117.180(d)).

What the person must do or oversee (117.180(a)). Preparation of the food safety plan; validation of the preventive controls; the written justification for validating beyond the first 90 calendar days of production; the determination that validation is not required; review of records; the written justification for reviewing monitoring and corrective action records beyond 7 working days; reanalysis of the food safety plan; and the determination that reanalysis and any additional validation can be completed beyond the first 90 calendar days.

A distinct role in the same section: a qualified auditor must conduct an onsite audit, and must have the technical expertise obtained through education, training or experience necessary to perform the auditing function (117.180(b), (c)(2)).

ideal_answer:
Exempt from reporting (21 CFR 806.1(b)). Four categories are exempt from Part 806's reporting requirements: actions taken to improve the performance or quality of a device that do not reduce a risk to health or remedy a violation of the act; market withdrawal as defined in 806.2(i); routine servicing as defined in 806.2(l); and stock recovery as defined in 806.2(m). Separately, a correction or removal need not be reported where the information has already been provided as set out in 806.10(f) (806.10(a)(2)).

Records still required (806.20). A manufacturer or importer who initiates a correction or removal not required to be reported under 806.10 must keep a record of it (806.20(a)). The record must contain the device's brand, common or usual name, classification, product code and intended use; the UDI or other identification and the lot or serial number; a description of the events giving rise to the information and the action taken; the justification for not reporting, containing conclusions and any follow-ups and reviewed and evaluated by a designated person; and copies of all communications regarding the action (806.20(b)).

Retention (806.20(c)). These records must be retained for 2 years beyond the expected life of the device, even if the manufacturer or importer has ceased to manufacture or import it.

The justification requirement is the point: an exempt action is not an unrecorded action, and the decision not to report must itself be documented and reviewed.

ideal_answer:
Part 11 sets the criteria under which FDA considers electronic records, electronic signatures and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records to be trustworthy, reliable and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten signatures on paper (21 CFR 11.1(a)).

It applies to records in electronic form that are created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirements set forth in agency regulations, and to electronic records submitted to the agency under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (11.1(b)). Where electronic signatures and their associated records meet this part, FDA considers them equivalent to full handwritten signatures and other general signings required by agency regulations, unless specifically excepted (11.1(c)). Electronic records meeting this part may be used in lieu of paper records, in accordance with 11.2, unless paper records are specifically required (11.1(d)). Systems, controls and attendant documentation must be readily available for, and subject to, FDA inspection (11.1(e)).

Exclusions. Part 11 does not apply to records required to be established or maintained by 1.326 through 1.368, by part 117, by part 507, by part 112, or by subpart L of part 1; records satisfying those requirements that are also required under other statutory provisions or regulations remain subject to part 11 (11.1(f), (i)-(l)). It also does not apply to electronic signatures obtained under 101.11(d) or 101.8(d) (11.1(g), (h)).

ideal_answer:
Both can apply, and which requirements you must meet is settled by 21 CFR Part 4, subpart A, not by choosing between Part 211 and Part 820.

Part 4 applies to combination products and establishes which CGMP requirements apply to them (4.1). Under 4.3 the requirements attach to the constituent parts: parts 210 and 211 apply to a combination product including a drug constituent part other than a medical gas (4.3(a)); part 820 applies to one including a device constituent part (4.3(b)); parts 600 through 680 where there is a biological product constituent part (4.3(c)); part 1271 where there is an HCT/P (4.3(d)); and part 213 where the drug constituent part is a medical gas (4.3(e)). For a drug-device combination product, both the drug CGMP and the device QMSR requirements are therefore engaged.

For a single-entity or co-packaged product, 4.4(a) then allows compliance to be achieved either by satisfying the specifics of each set of regulations listed in 4.3 as they apply to each constituent part, or by the streamlined route in 4.4(b): demonstrate compliance with one system and additionally satisfy a defined list of provisions from the other.

So the answer is not "211" or "820" but: both regimes are engaged, and Part 4 lets you satisfy them through one operating system plus the specified provisions of the other.

Subpart D of 21 CFR Part 50 adds the safeguards. An IRB must review clinical investigations involving children and approve only those satisfying the criteria of 50.51, 50.52 or 50.53 and the conditions of all other applicable sections of the subpart (50.50).

The three risk and benefit categories. Where no greater than minimal risk is presented, children may be involved only if the IRB finds that no greater than minimal risk is presented and that adequate provisions are made for assent and parental permission (50.51). Where more than minimal risk is presented by an intervention holding out the prospect of direct benefit to the individual subject, or by a monitoring procedure likely to contribute to the subject's well-being, the IRB must find that the risk is justified by the anticipated benefit (50.52(a)). Where more than minimal risk is presented with no prospect of direct benefit but the investigation is likely to yield generalizable knowledge about the subjects' disorder or condition, the IRB must find that the risk represents a minor increase over minimal risk (50.53(a)).

Assent and permission (50.55). In addition to the other determinations, the IRB must determine that adequate provisions are made for soliciting the assent of the children where, in its judgment, they are capable of providing it, and for the permission of their parents or guardians.

Wards (50.56). Children who are wards may be included in investigations approved under 50.53 or 50.54 only where these are related to their status as wards, or conducted in settings where most child subjects are not wards; the IRB must then require appointment of an advocate for each ward, who must be independent of the investigation, the investigators and the guardian organization.

Two regimes apply.

Medicated feed CGMP (21 CFR Part 225). Section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Act deems a drug, including a drug contained in a medicated feed, adulterated if the methods, facilities or controls used in its manufacture, processing, packing or holding do not conform to current good manufacturing practice (225.1(a)). Part 225 sets the criteria for determining whether the manufacture of a medicated feed complies, and applies to all types of facilities and equipment used in producing medicated feeds (225.1(b)(1)). Which sections apply depends on licensing: 225.10 through 225.115 apply to facilities manufacturing medicated feeds for which an approved medicated feed mill license is required, and 225.120 through 225.202 to facilities manufacturing solely feeds for which no licence is required (225.1(b)(2)). Qualified personnel with adequate training and supervision are required, and all employees involved must understand the operations they perform, including the location and proper use of equipment (225.10).

Veterinary feed directive drugs (558.6). A VFD feed or combination VFD feed may be fed to animals only by or upon a lawful VFD issued by a licensed veterinarian (558.6(a)(1)), and the issuing veterinarian must be licensed to practise veterinary medicine (558.6(b)(1)(i)). All labeling and advertising for VFD drugs and feeds containing them must prominently and conspicuously display the cautionary statement that federal law restricts the medicated feed to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian (558.6(a)(6)).

Distributor records. A distributor must keep records of the receipt and distribution of all medicated animal feed containing a VFD drug for 2 years, and a distributor that also manufactures the feed must keep VFD feed manufacturing records for 1 year in accordance with Part 225, available to FDA on request (558.6(c)(3), (c)(4)).

The requirement. So responsibility attaches to the receiving facility, and it attaches only where the facility has itself identified such a hazard and relies on a control applied in the supply chain. The program must be written (507.105(b)).

When it does not apply. A receiving facility that is an importer, is in compliance with the foreign supplier verification requirements of part 1 subpart L, and has documentation of verification activities conducted under 1.506(e) providing assurance that the hazards requiring a supply-chain-applied control have been significantly minimized or prevented, need not conduct supplier verification activities for that raw material or ingredient (507.105(a)(2)). The subpart's requirements also do not apply to animal food supplied for research or evaluation use, on the conditions set out in 507.105(a)(3).

Records (507.175). The records documenting the program are subject to subpart F (507.175(a)), and the receiving facility must document, as applicable: the written supply-chain program; documentation of FSVP compliance where it is an importer; approval of a supplier; the determination of the appropriate supplier verification activities; other verification activities based on supplier performance and risk; the written assurance where an alternative activity is used for a supplier that is a qualified facility; and verification of a supply-chain-applied control applied by an entity other than the supplier (507.175(c)).

Which foods. Except as otherwise specified in the subpart, the requirements apply to persons who manufacture, process, pack or hold foods that appear on the list of foods for which additional traceability records are required under section 204(d)(2) of FSMA - the Food Traceability List, which FDA publishes on its website (21 CFR 1.1300).

Traceability plan (1.1315(a)). If you are subject to the subpart you must establish and maintain a traceability plan containing a description of the procedures you use to maintain the required records, including their format and location; the procedures you use to identify foods on the List that you handle; how you assign traceability lot codes in accordance with 1.1320; and, if you grow or raise a listed food other than eggs, a farm map showing the location and name of each field or growing area, with geographic coordinates (1.1315(a)(5)(i)).

Traceability lot codes (1.1320). You must assign a traceability lot code when you initially pack a raw agricultural commodity other than a food obtained from a fishing vessel, perform the first land-based receiving of a food obtained from a fishing vessel, or transform a food. You must not establish a new code when conducting other activities such as shipping.

Records at each event (1.1340 and the neighbouring sections). For each traceability lot you ship, you must maintain records containing the specified information and linking it to the traceability lot, including the date you shipped the food. Parallel sections carry the records for harvesting and cooling, initial packing, first land-based receiving, receiving and transformation, so which records you keep depends on which of those events you perform.

Two different routes, and it is worth separating them.

General exceptions (21 CFR 801.30). Some devices are excepted from the UDI labelling requirement of 801.20 by the regulation itself, with no application needed - a device within one or more of the 801.30(a) exceptions is simply not required to bear a UDI. They include a finished device manufactured and labeled before the compliance date established for 801.20 for that device, which exception expires 3 years after that date (801.30(a)(1)); individual single-use devices of a single version or model distributed together in a single device package, not intended for individual commercial distribution and not implantable, though the package itself is not excepted (801.30(a)(3)); and a device held by the Strategic National Stockpile granted an exception under 801.128(f)(2) (801.30(a)(9)).

Requesting an exception or alternative (801.55). Where no general exception applies, a labeler may submit a written request for an exception from, or an alternative to, the requirement of 801.20 or any other requirement of the subpart, for a specified device or type of device (801.55(a)). The request must identify the devices that would be subject to it and the provisions that are its subject, provide if known the number of labelers and devices that would be affected, and provide other information the Center Director needs to clarify the scope and effects (801.55(a)(1), (2), (5), (6)). It is submitted as 801.55(b) directs.

The criteria FDA applies (801.55(c)). The Center Director may grant an exception or alternative, in response to a request or on his or her own initiative, on determining that an exception is appropriate because the requirements of the subpart are not technologically feasible, or that an alternative would provide for more accurate, precise or rapid device identification or would better ensure the safety or effectiveness of the device.

IND content (21 CFR 312.23). A sponsor intending to conduct a clinical investigation subject to the part must submit an Investigational New Drug Application including, in the order the section sets out, a cover sheet on Form FDA-1571 (312.23(a)(1)), followed by the remaining required sections - the table of contents, introductory statement and general investigational plan, investigator's brochure, protocols, chemistry, manufacturing and control information, pharmacology and toxicology information, previous human experience and any additional information. The amount of information required depends on the scope of the proposed investigation (312.23(a)(7)(ii)).

Definitions (312.32(a)). Adverse event means any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of a drug in humans, whether or not considered drug related. Suspected adverse reaction means any adverse event for which there is a reasonable possibility that the drug caused it, "reasonable possibility" meaning there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship.

Reporting (312.32(c)). The sponsor must notify FDA and all participating investigators in an IND safety report of potential serious risks, including any suspected adverse reaction that is both serious and unexpected, reporting an adverse event as a suspected adverse reaction only where there is evidence suggesting a causal relationship (312.32(c)(1)(i)); and any clinically important increase in the rate of a serious suspected adverse reaction over that listed in the protocol or investigator brochure (312.32(c)(1)(iv)).

Timeframes. The 15-calendar-day clock applies to IND safety reports under 312.32(c)(1). For an unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction, the sponsor must also notify FDA as soon as possible and in no case later than 7 calendar days (312.32(c)(2)).

Who must submit, and for which devices. The labeler of a device must provide the information required by subpart E for each version or model required to bear a unique device identifier (21 CFR 830.300(a)). A labeler that voluntarily includes a UDI on a label under 801.40 may also submit information voluntarily (830.300(b)), and FDA may reject or remove device identification data in the circumstances set out in 830.300(c).

What must be submitted. The contact for device identification designated under 830.320(a) must provide FDA with the information specified in 830.310 for each version or model required to bear a UDI - the data elements concerning the labeler (830.310(a)) and concerning the device (830.310(b)), which include the Global Medical Device Nomenclature term or code (830.310(b)(13)).

How. Each labeler must designate an individual as the point of contact with FDA on matters relating to device identification, responsible for ensuring FDA is provided with the required information (830.320(a)). All information must be submitted electronically to FDA's Global Unique Device Identification Database (GUDID) in a format FDA can process, review and archive, unless the labeler has obtained a waiver (830.320(b)). A waiver may be requested by letter to the appropriate Center Director explaining why electronic submission is not technologically feasible, and a labeler whose establishment holds a waiver from electronic registration and listing under section 510(p) of the Act is deemed to have one for UDI data (830.320(c)(1), (2)).

Timeframe. A labeler operating under a waiver must send the 830.310 information by letter within the time permitted by 830.330 (830.320(c)(3)), which is the section that fixes the submission deadline tied to the date the device is labeled.

Scope (21 CFR 4.100). Subpart B identifies the postmarketing safety reporting requirements for combination product applicants and constituent part applicants. It does not apply to investigational combination products, to combination products that have not received marketing authorization, or to persons other than those applicants (4.100(b)). It supplements and does not supersede other provisions of the chapter, including parts 314, 600, 606, 803 and 806, unless a regulation explicitly provides otherwise (4.100(c)).

Which requirements apply (4.102). The reporting requirements that apply turn on what you are: if you are a constituent part applicant, the requirements identified in the section apply to your constituent part; if you are a combination product applicant, the requirements identified apply to the combination product (4.102(a)). 4.102(b) then identifies the reporting requirements applicable to both kinds of applicant, by application type.

Shared responsibilities (4.103). When you receive information regarding an event involving a death or serious injury as described in 803.3, or an adverse experience as described in 314.80(a) or 600.80(a), associated with the combination product, you must provide that information to the other constituent part applicant(s) - and you must maintain records of the information you provide (4.103(b)).

How reports are submitted (4.104). A constituent part applicant submits postmarketing safety reports in accordance with the regulations identified in 4.102(b) applicable to its product based on application type (4.104(a)). A combination product applicant submits the reports required under 4.102 in the manner specified in the regulation applicable to the type of report, subject to the exceptions 4.104(b) sets out.

Registration (21 CFR 108.35(c)(1)). A commercial processor, when first engaging in the manufacture, processing or packing of thermally processed low-acid foods in hermetically sealed containers in any State as defined in section 201(a)(1) of the Act, must register with FDA within the time the paragraph specifies, providing the information it requires for the establishment.

Process adherence (108.35(c)(3)). A commercial processor must process each low-acid food in each container size in conformity with at least the scheduled processes and modifications filed (108.35(c)(3)(i)), and must, when FDA requests in writing, provide FDA with any information concerning processes and procedures that is deemed necessary to determine the adequacy of the process (108.35(c)(3)(ii)).

The definitions in 113.3 apply to the terms used in the section (108.35(b)).

108.35(c) is headed “Registration and process filing”, so the section also carries a process-filing obligation, and the adherence requirement above refers to scheduled processes already filed with FDA. The filing paragraph itself is not among the provisions supplied here, so its terms and deadlines cannot be stated from this evidence.

When a master manufacturing record is required. You must prepare and follow a written master manufacturing record for each unique formulation of dietary supplement that you manufacture, and for each batch size, to ensure uniformity in the finished batch from batch to batch (21 CFR 111.205(a)). So the trigger is the combination of formulation and batch size: a new formulation needs its own MMR, and so does a different batch size of the same formulation.

What it must contain. The MMR must identify specifications for the points, steps or stages in the manufacturing process where control is necessary to ensure the quality of the dietary supplement and that it is packaged and labeled as specified in the record (111.205(b)(1)); and must establish controls and procedures to ensure that each batch meets those specifications (111.205(b)(2)).

How the batch production record relates to it. A batch production record must be prepared every time you manufacture a batch (111.255(a)) and must include complete information relating to the production and control of that batch (111.255(b)). Critically, the BPR must accurately follow the appropriate master manufacturing record, and you must perform each step in the production of the batch (111.255(c)).

So the MMR is the per-formulation, per-batch-size template; the BPR is the per-batch execution record that must track it. Both must be made and kept in accordance with subpart P (111.205(c), 111.255(d)).

The link is established by 21 CFR 820.10(b)(3), and the complaints must be reported to FDA under Part 803.

820.10(b) requires a manufacturer to comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in Title 21 in order to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 clauses. Specifically, for Clause 8.2.3 in ISO 13485, Reporting to regulatory authorities, the manufacturer must notify FDA of complaints that meet the reporting criteria of part 803 of this chapter (820.10(b)(3)).

So Part 820 does not itself set the reporting criteria or the timeframes: 820.10(b)(3) is the bridge, and the substantive medical device reporting requirements live in Part 803.

Note the neighbouring cross-reference, which is often confused with this one: advisory notices are handled under Part 806, by way of 820.10(b)(4).

The record control section is 21 CFR 820.35, and the requirement is that the UDI be recorded for each medical device or batch of medical devices.

820.35 adds FDA-specified content on top of Clause 4.2.5 in ISO 13485, Control of Records, incorporated by reference at 820.7. Within it, 820.35(c), Unique Device Identification, provides that in addition to the requirements of Clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.8 and 7.5.9 in ISO 13485, the UDI must be recorded for each medical device or batch of medical devices.

The UDI also appears as a required element of two other record types in the same section: a complaint record must include any UDI or universal product code and any other device identification (820.35(a)(3)), and a servicing record must include the same (820.35(b)(2)).

The obligation to assign the identifier in the first place sits elsewhere - 820.10(b)(1) requires a documented system to assign unique device identification in accordance with Part 830.

The permitted activities (21 CFR 117.410(b)). The appropriate supplier verification activities for raw materials and other ingredients are onsite audits (117.410(b)(1)); sampling and testing; review of the supplier's relevant food safety records (117.410(b)(3)); and other appropriate activities based on supplier performance and the risk associated with the raw material or ingredient (117.410(b)(4)).

How the appropriate one is selected (117.410(d)(1)). In approving suppliers and determining the appropriate verification activities and the frequency with which they are conducted, you must consider the hazard analysis of the food, including the nature of the hazard controlled before receipt of the raw material or ingredient (117.410(d)(1)(i)); and the supplier's food safety history relevant to the materials you receive from it, including available information about results from testing for hazards and audit results relating to the safety of the food (117.410(d)(1)(iii)(C)), among the other listed factors. Suppliers must be approved in accordance with 117.410(d) and that approval documented before receiving materials from them (117.420(a)).

When the activity must be conducted (117.430). Except as 117.430(c), (d) or (e) provide, one or more of the activities specified in 117.410(b), as determined under 117.410(d), must be conducted for each supplier before using the raw material or ingredient and periodically thereafter.

The severe-hazard rule. Where a hazard will be controlled by the supplier and is one for which there is a reasonable probability that exposure would result in serious adverse health consequences or death, the appropriate verification activity is an onsite audit of the supplier (117.430(b)(1), (b)(1)(i)). That requirement does not apply where there is a written determination that other verification activities, or less frequent onsite auditing, provide adequate assurance that the hazards are controlled (117.430(b)(2)).

21 CFR 50.24 permits it only on a defined set of IRB findings. The IRB responsible for review, approval and continuing review may approve the investigation without requiring informed consent from all subjects only if it finds, with the concurrence of a licensed physician who is a member of or consultant to the IRB and is not otherwise participating, all of the following (50.24(a)).

The conditions. Obtaining informed consent is not feasible because the subjects will not be able to give it as a result of their medical condition, and the intervention under investigation must be administered before consent from their legally authorized representatives is feasible (50.24(a)(2)(i), (ii)). Participation holds out the prospect of direct benefit to the subjects because they are facing a life-threatening situation that necessitates intervention (50.24(a)(3)(i)). And the investigation could not practicably be carried out without the waiver (50.24(a)(4)).

Community consultation and public disclosure (50.24(a)(7)). Additional protections are required, including public disclosure to the communities in which the investigation will be conducted and from which subjects will be drawn, before initiation, of the plans for the investigation and its risks and expected benefits (50.24(a)(7)(ii)); and public disclosure of sufficient information after completion to apprise the community and researchers of the study, including the demographic characteristics of the research population, and its results (50.24(a)(7)(iii)).

Two procedural requirements. Protocols involving this exception must be performed under a separate IND or IDE that clearly identifies them as protocols that may include subjects who are unable to consent (50.24(d)). And if an IRB determines it cannot approve the investigation because it does not meet the 50.24(a) criteria or because of other relevant ethical concerns, it must document its findings and provide them promptly as the paragraph directs (50.24(e)).

Identify and quarantine first. You must identify and quarantine returned dietary supplements until quality control personnel conduct a material review and make a disposition decision (21 CFR 111.510). Nothing happens to the returned product until that review is done.

The default is disposal. You must destroy, or otherwise suitably dispose of, any returned dietary supplement unless the outcome of the material review and disposition decision is that quality control personnel approve the salvage of the product for redistribution, or approve it for reprocessing (111.515(a), (b)).

Salvage. You may salvage a returned dietary supplement only if quality control personnel conduct a material review and make a disposition decision to allow the salvage (111.520). There is no route to redistribution that bypasses that decision.

Reprocessing. Where quality control personnel approve reprocessing, you must ensure that any reprocessed returned dietary supplements meet all product specifications established in accordance with 111.70(e), and quality control personnel must approve or reject the release for distribution of the reprocessed product (111.525(a), (b)).

So the decision-maker at every branch is quality control personnel, and the sequence is quarantine, material review, then disposal unless salvage or reprocessing is approved.

The obligation to determine. You must determine whether the specifications you establish under 21 CFR 111.70 are met (111.73). For a finished batch that includes verifying identity: you must conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify the identity of any component that is a dietary ingredient, unless the agency has exempted you on petition (111.75(a)(1)(i)); and you must monitor the in-process points, steps or stages where control is necessary to determine whether in-process specifications are met (111.75(b)).

Who decides. Quality control personnel must conduct all required material reviews and make all required disposition decisions (111.87). So a failed identity specification goes to quality control personnel for material review and disposition - not to production.

What may then be done (111.90). You must not reprocess a rejected dietary supplement, or treat or make an in-process adjustment to a component, packaging or label to make it suitable for use, unless the conditions 111.90(a) sets out are satisfied. Reprocessing is therefore conditional, not a default remedy for a failed specification.

The quality control role runs through the section generally: quality control personnel must review and approve the documentation supporting supplier qualification (111.75(a)(2)(ii)(E)), the documentation under 111.75(c)(3) (111.75(c)(4)), and any documented exemption of a product specification from the verification requirements (111.75(d)(1), (d)(2)).

You must act promptly. Under 21 CFR 1.508(a), if you determine that a foreign supplier of food you import does not produce the food in compliance with processes and procedures that provide at least the same level of public health protection as those required under section 418 or 419 of the Act, or produces food that is adulterated or misbranded with respect to allergen labeling, you must promptly take appropriate corrective action. What is appropriate depends on the nature of the hazard and the supplier's non-compliance.

Where you learn of it by another route (1.508(b)). If you make that determination by means other than the verification activities conducted under 1.506 or 1.511(c), or a reevaluation under 1.505(c) or (d), you must promptly investigate to determine whether your FSVP is adequate and, when appropriate, modify it. So learning of a failure outside your planned verification is itself a trigger to test the programme, not only the supplier.

What this does not displace (1.508(c)). The section does not limit your obligations under other laws enforced by FDA, such as those relating to product recalls. Corrective action under FSVP is in addition to, not instead of, any recall or reporting duty.

So three things follow: prompt corrective action on the supplier relationship, investigation of whether the FSVP itself is adequate with modification where needed, and separate compliance with any recall obligation.

Written procedures first. You must establish and follow written procedures to fulfil the requirements of subpart O (21 CFR 111.553).

Review and investigation (111.560(a)). A qualified person must review all product complaints to determine whether the complaint involves a possible failure of a dietary supplement to meet any of its specifications, or any other requirement of Part 111, including those which, if not met, may result in a risk of illness or injury (111.560(a)(1)); and must investigate any complaint that does involve such a possible failure (111.560(a)(2)).

Quality control's role (111.560(b)). Quality control personnel must review and approve the decisions about whether to investigate a product complaint, and must review and approve the findings and follow-up action of any investigation performed. So the qualified person screens and investigates; quality control personnel approve both the decision and the outcome.

Scope of the work (111.560(c)). The review and investigation by the qualified person, the quality control review of whether to investigate, and the findings and follow-up action of any investigation must extend to all relevant batches and records - not only the batch complained of.

No. A new edition does not automatically become the standard required by Part 820.

Incorporation by reference fixes a specific edition. 21 CFR 820.7 incorporates certain material by reference with the approval of the Director of the Federal Register under 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and 1 CFR part 51, and it names the editions precisely: ISO 9000:2015(E), Clause 3, Terms and definitions, Fourth edition, September 15, 2015, IBR approved for 820.3 (820.7(a)); and ISO 13485:2016(E), Medical devices - Quality management systems - Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016, IBR approved for 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35 and 820.45 (820.7(b)).

What that means in practice. The obligation under 820.10(a) is to document a quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 as incorporated - that is, the 2016 third edition named in 820.7(b). A later edition published by ISO is not what the regulation points to, and it does not displace the named edition. FDA would have to amend 820.7 through rulemaking, with the Federal Register approval the section describes, for a new edition to become the incorporated standard.

So until that happens, the 2016 third edition remains the requirement, whatever edition is current at ISO.

The controls. In addition to the requirements of Clause 7.5.1 of ISO 13485, Control of production and service provision, incorporated by reference at 21 CFR 820.7, each manufacturer must document and maintain procedures giving a detailed description of the activities to ensure the integrity, inspection, storage and operations for labeling and packaging during the customary conditions of processing, storage, handling and distribution (820.45).

Preventing mixups (820.45(c)). The manufacturer must ensure that labeling and packaging operations have been established and maintained to prevent mixups, including but not limited to inspection of the labeling and packaging before use to assure that all devices have correct labeling and packaging as specified in the medical device file.

What must be documented. The results of that labeling inspection must be documented in accordance with Clause 4.2.5 of ISO 13485 (820.45(c)), and the release of the labeling for use must likewise be documented in accordance with Clause 4.2.5 (820.45(b)).

What the examination must cover (820.45(a)). Labeling and packaging must be examined for accuracy prior to release or storage where applicable, including the correct unique device identifier or universal product code or other device identification, the expiration date, the storage instructions, the handling instructions and any additional processing instructions.

It depends which specification you mean, and for the identity of a dietary ingredient the answer is no.

Identity of a dietary ingredient. You must conduct at least one appropriate test or examination to verify the identity of any component that is a dietary ingredient, unless you petition the agency under 21 CFR 111.75(a)(1)(ii) and the agency exempts you (111.75(a)(1)(i)). A supplier certificate of analysis does not discharge this; the only route to relying on something else is a petition under 21 CFR 10.30 setting out the scientific rationale with supporting data for the proposed alternative testing (111.75(a)(1)(ii)).

Other component specifications. For components other than the identity of a dietary ingredient, you may rely on a certificate of analysis from the supplier, but only on conditions (111.75(a)(2)(ii)): you must first qualify the supplier by establishing the reliability of its certificate through confirmation of the results of the supplier's tests or examinations (A); the certificate must include a description of the test or examination methods used, the limits of the tests, and the actual results (B); and you must periodically re-confirm the supplier's certificate (D).

What you must do in any event. You must visually examine each immediate container or grouping of containers in a shipment for appropriate content label, container damage or broken seals, to determine whether the container condition may have resulted in contamination or deterioration (111.155(a)); and visually examine the supplier's invoice, guarantee or certification to ensure the components are consistent with your purchase order (111.155(b)).

Where the operating system has been shown to comply with the drug CGMP requirements, or the medical gas CGMP requirements as applicable, 21 CFR 4.4(b)(1) requires that specified clauses of ISO 13485 and provisions of Part 820 also be satisfied. They cover general requirements and management responsibility, design and development, purchasing, analysis of data and improvement including complaint handling, installation activities and servicing activities.

The election runs the other way too. Where instead the system has been shown to comply with the QMSR requirements for devices, specified drug CGMP provisions must also be satisfied (4.4(b)(2)) - including 211.84 on testing and approval or rejection of components, containers and closures (4.4(b)(2)(i)) and 211.132 on tamper-evident packaging for OTC human drug products (4.4(b)(2)(iii)). Where the drug constituent part is a medical gas, the additions come from the medical gas CGMP requirements instead (4.4(b)(3)).

Two related rules in the same section. Where constituent parts are manufactured at separate facilities, the CGMP requirements apply as 4.4(c) provides for that period. And the requirements of the subpart and of parts 210, 211, 213, 820, 600 through 680 and 1271 listed in 4.3 supplement, and do not supersede, each other unless the regulations explicitly provide otherwise, with the more specifically applicable requirement governing a conflict (4.4(e)).
