The Act and the applicable FDA regulations govern, not the standard.

21 CFR 820.1(b) sets out the order of precedence. The QMSR in Part 820 supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise. To the extent that any applicable requirements in Part 820 conflict with requirements in other parts of the chapter, the requirements specifically applicable to the device in question supersede the more generally applicable ones. And, to the extent that any clauses of ISO 13485 - incorporated by reference at 820.7 - conflict with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or with FDA regulations, the Act and those regulations prevail.

So incorporation by reference does not give the standard priority over US law. ISO 13485 is binding because 820.10(a) requires a documented quality management system complying with its applicable requirements, but where its text and a statutory or regulatory requirement cannot both be satisfied, the statutory or regulatory requirement is the one to follow.

The practical consequence is that the standard cannot be read as relaxing anything the Act or a Title 21 regulation requires, and 820.10(b) reinforces this by expressly routing certain clauses to the other Title 21 parts that govern them.

The design and development requirements are mandatory for manufacturers of class II and class III devices, and for the class I devices the section lists.

21 CFR 820.10(c) requires manufacturers of class II devices, class III devices, and those class I devices listed in 820.10(c)(1) and in table 1 to 820.10(c)(2), to comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its subclauses in ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7. The class I devices brought in by 820.10(c)(1) are those automated with computer software, together with the devices listed in the table at 820.10(c)(2).

So the position for class I is conditional rather than general: a class I device is outside 820.10(c) unless it is automated with computer software or appears in that table.

This sits alongside the baseline duty in 820.10(a), which applies to every manufacturer subject to the part as described by 820.1(a): document a quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 and the other applicable requirements of the part.

Dual-column labelling is required. A product packaged and sold individually that contains at least 200 percent and up to and including 300 percent of the applicable reference amount customarily consumed must provide an additional column within the Nutrition Facts label listing the quantitative amounts and percent Daily Values for the entire package, as well as the per-serving column (21 CFR 101.9(b)(12)(i)). So the label carries both: per serving and per container.

Two exceptions apply. The provision does not apply to products that meet the requirements to use the tabular format, or those that meet the requirements to use the linear format, both of which 101.9(b)(12)(i)(A) identifies by cross-reference to the format provisions elsewhere in the section. Nor does it apply to raw fruits, vegetables and seafood for which voluntary nutrition labeling is provided in the product labeling or advertising, or when claims are made about the product (101.9(b)(12)(i)(B)).

The general obligation behind this is 101.9(a): nutrition information must be provided for all products intended for human consumption and offered for sale unless an exemption is provided for the product in that section's exemptions paragraph.

Because the regulation requires it, and the requirement is about keeping a record of the thinking as much as the outcome.

In plain terms: when someone complains that a device, its labeling or its packaging may not have met its specifications, the manufacturer has to look into it and write down what it found. That is how a pattern of failures becomes visible before it harms someone, and how FDA can see that the manufacturer noticed.

What requires it: 21 CFR 820.35(a). In addition to Clause 8.2.2 in ISO 13485, Complaint Handling - incorporated by reference at 820.7 - the manufacturer must maintain records of the review, evaluation and investigation of any complaint involving the possible failure of a device, labeling or packaging to meet any of its specifications. The record must include the name of the device, the date the complaint was received, any UDI or UPC and other device identification, the complainant's name, address and phone number, the nature and details of the complaint, any correction or corrective action taken, and any reply to the complainant (820.35(a)(1) through (7)).

So the duty to investigate comes from the incorporated standard's complaint handling clause; 820.35(a) is the Part 820 provision that makes the record of that investigation, and its contents, mandatory.

How the exemption works. A device which, because of any potentiality for harmful effect, the method of its use, or the collateral measures necessary to its use, is not safe except under the supervision of a licensed practitioner - and for which adequate directions for lay use cannot be written - is exempt from the adequate directions for use requirement, provided the conditions of 21 CFR 801.109 are met.

The conditions. The device must be sold only to, or on the prescription or other order of, such a practitioner for use in the course of his professional practice (801.109(a)(2)). Its label must bear the symbol statement "Rx only" or "℞ only", or the statement "Caution: Federal law restricts this device to sale by or on the order of a ___", the blank filled with "physician", "dentist", "veterinarian" or the descriptive designation of the practitioner licensed to use or order the device (801.109(b)(1)).

Labeling. Labeling on or within the package from which the device is dispensed must bear information for use, including indications, effects, routes, methods, and frequency and duration of administration, and any relevant hazards, contraindications, side effects and precautions under which practitioners can use the device safely (801.109(c)).

Advertising and other labeling. Any labeling as defined in section 201(m) of the Act, whether or not on or within the package, distributed by or on behalf of the manufacturer, packer or distributor and furnishing information for use of the device, must meet the conditions 801.109(d) sets out. And all labeling other than labels and cartons bearing information for use must also bear the date of issuance or of the latest revision (801.109(e)).

The FDA supplements are the provisions that say "in addition to" a clause of the standard, or that impose a Title 21 duty on top of it. Three sections do that.

820.10(b) routes specific clauses to other Title 21 parts: for Clause 7.5.8, Identification, a documented system to assign unique device identification in accordance with Part 830 (820.10(b)(1)); for Clause 7.5.9.1, Traceability, documented traceability procedures in accordance with Part 821 if applicable (820.10(b)(2)); for Clause 8.2.3, Reporting to regulatory authorities, notification to FDA of complaints meeting the reporting criteria of Part 803 (820.10(b)(3)). The remaining paragraphs of 820.10 add FDA's own conditions on design and development, on devices that support or sustain life, and on enforcement.

820.35 adds record content on top of Clause 4.2.5, Control of Records: the specified contents of a complaint record in addition to Clause 8.2.2 (820.35(a)); the minimum servicing record contents in adhering to Clause 7.5.4 (820.35(b)); and, in addition to Clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.8 and 7.5.9, that the UDI be recorded for each device or batch of devices (820.35(c)).

820.45 adds labeling and packaging controls on top of Clause 7.5.1, Control of production and service provision - documented procedures describing the activities that ensure integrity, inspection, storage and operations for labeling and packaging, and the accuracy examination 820.45(a) specifies.

Everything else reaches the manufacturer by incorporation by reference: 820.10(a) requires a documented quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485, incorporated at 820.7, and the balance of the quality system is the standard's, not FDA's own text.

The first and third are defined in the evidence - 101.14(a)(1) defines a health claim and 101.93 covers structure/function statements and their notification - but the qualified health claim is a construct of FDA enforcement discretion articulated in guidance, and neither the significant-scientific-agreement standard nor the qualified-claim disclaimer language is in the packed provision text. An IRB may use the expedited review procedure for either or both of two things (21 CFR 56.110(b)): some or all of the research appearing on the list FDA has established and published in the Federal Register, where the reviewer finds it involves no more than minimal risk (56.110(b)(1)); and minor changes in previously approved research during the period, of 1 year or less, for which approval is authorized.

Who may conduct it. Under the expedited procedure the review may be carried out by the IRB chairperson, or by one or more experienced reviewers designated by the chairperson from among the members of the IRB (56.110(b)).

Where the list comes from. FDA has established and published in the Federal Register a list of categories of research that may be reviewed through an expedited procedure, amended as appropriate by periodic republication (56.110(a)). So the first limb is not an open judgement about risk - the research has to fall within a published category and be found to involve no more than minimal risk.

Two controls on the procedure. Each IRB using it must adopt a method for keeping all members advised of research proposals approved under it (56.110(c)); and FDA may restrict, suspend or terminate an institution's or IRB's use of the procedure when necessary to protect the rights or welfare of subjects (56.110(d)).

The standard. FDA determines that a device is substantially equivalent to a predicate device using the criteria in 21 CFR 807.100(b). The device must have the same intended use as the predicate (807.100(b)(1)); and it must either have the same technological characteristics as the predicate (807.100(b)(2)(i)), or have different technological characteristics - a significant change in materials, design, energy source or other features - provided that the data submitted establishes substantial equivalence and contains information, including clinical data if the Commissioner deems it necessary, demonstrating the device is as safe and as effective as a legally marketed device, and that it does not raise different questions of safety and effectiveness than the predicate (807.100(b)(2)(ii)(A) through (C)).

A condition on the predicate. The predicate must not have been removed from the market at the Commissioner's initiative, and must not have been determined to be misbranded or adulterated by judicial order (807.100(b)(3)).

How it is determined procedurally (807.100(a)). After reviewing a premarket notification FDA will issue an order declaring the device substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate; or declaring it not substantially equivalent to any legally marketed predicate; or request additional information; or withhold the decision until a certification or disclosure statement is submitted under Part 54; or advise the applicant that the notification is not required.

The practical consequence: until the applicant receives an order declaring the device substantially equivalent, it may not proceed to market the device (807.100(a)(5)).

No. The provisions of Part 820 do not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, although such manufacturers are encouraged to consider the provisions of the regulation as appropriate (21 CFR 820.1(a)(2)).

The reason sits in what the part governs. Its requirements govern the methods used in, and the facilities and controls used for, the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use (820.1(a)). The unit of regulation is the finished device, so a supplier of a component or part falls outside it in its own right.

Two qualifications worth stating. The encouragement in 820.1(a)(2) is not a requirement, and nothing in the part makes a component manufacturer subject to it voluntarily. But a finished device manufacturer remains responsible for its own quality management system under 820.10(a), and the purchasing and supplier controls that reach it through ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, apply to the components it buys - so component quality is controlled through the finished device manufacturer rather than directly.

Note the contrast with the neighbouring carve-outs in the same paragraph: blood and blood components are excluded and sent to subchapter F (820.1(a)(3)), while HCT/Ps that are devices are expressly brought in (820.1(a)(4)).

No. The provisions of Part 820 do not apply to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or for further manufacturing; such manufacturers are subject to subchapter F of this chapter (21 CFR 820.1(a)(3)).

Subchapter F is where the blood regulations sit, including the CGMP requirements for blood and blood components in Part 606. So the exclusion is not an absence of regulation - it is a redirection to a different regime.

The boundary matters because the part's own scope is the finished device: its requirements govern the methods, facilities and controls used for the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use (820.1(a)).

Contrast the adjacent carve-outs, which run in different directions. Manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices are also outside the part, though encouraged to consider its provisions as appropriate (820.1(a)(2)). But manufacturers of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products that are devices are expressly within it (820.1(a)(4)). So "blood" and "HCT/P" are treated oppositely, and the distinction is drawn by 820.1(a) itself.

Who is subject. Persons who manufacture, process, pack, transport, distribute, receive, hold or import food in the United States are subject to subpart J, unless they qualify for one of the exclusions in 21 CFR 1.327; a person conducting more than one type of activity at a location is required to keep records for each activity (1.326(a)). The obligation applies whether or not the food is being offered for or enters interstate commerce (1.326(b)).

Records of the immediate previous source (1.337(a)). A nontransporter must establish and maintain, for all food it receives: the name, address and telephone number and, if available, the fax number and email address of the nontransporter immediate previous source, domestic or foreign; an adequate description of the type of food, including brand name and specific variety; the date received; for persons who manufacture, process or pack food, the lot or code number or other identifier to the extent it exists; the quantity and how the food is packaged; and the same contact details for the transporter that brought the food.

Records of the immediate subsequent recipient (1.345(a)). The same set is required for food released: the recipient's contact details, an adequate description of the food including brand name and specific variety, the date released, the lot or code number where applicable, the quantity and packaging, and the contact details of the transporter that took the food. The records must also include information reasonably available to identify the specific source of each ingredient used to make every lot of finished product (1.345(b)).

The "adequate description" standard is specific: brand x cheddar cheese, not just cheese; romaine lettuce, not just lettuce.

Personnel (21 CFR 507.14). The management of the establishment must take reasonable measures and precautions to ensure that all persons working in direct contact with animal food, animal food-contact surfaces and animal food-packaging materials conform to hygienic practices and maintain cleanliness (507.14(a)). The methods include maintaining adequate personal cleanliness; washing hands thoroughly in an adequate hand-washing facility as necessary and appropriate to protect against contamination; removing or securing jewelry and other objects that might fall into animal food, equipment or containers; and storing clothing and other personal belongings away from areas where animal food is exposed or equipment and utensils are cleaned (507.14(b)).

Holding and distribution of human food by-products for use as animal food (507.28). By-products held for distribution as animal food must be held under conditions protecting against contamination: containers and equipment used to convey or hold them must be designed, constructed of appropriate material, cleaned as necessary and maintained so as to protect against contamination; the by-products must be held so as to protect against contamination from sources such as trash; and during holding they must be accurately identified (507.28(a)). Labeling identifying the product by its common or usual name must be affixed to or accompany the by-products when distributed (507.28(b)), and shipping containers such as totes, drums and tubs, and bulk vehicles used to distribute them, must be examined prior to use to protect against contamination (507.28(c)).

The subpart also carries requirements for plant and grounds, sanitation, water supply and plumbing, equipment and utensils, and processes and controls, each in its own section of subpart B.

Consultants advising on the manufacture, processing, packing or holding of drug products must have sufficient education, training and experience, or any combination thereof, to advise on the subject for which they are retained (21 CFR 211.34).

Records must be maintained stating the name, address and qualifications of any consultants and the type of service they provide (211.34).

So there are two obligations and both sit in the same short section: a qualification standard for the consultant, and a record of who they are and what they do.

Representative samples (21 CFR 111.80). You must collect representative samples of: each unique lot of components, packaging and labels you use, to determine whether they meet the specifications established under 111.70(b) and (d) and, as applicable, 111.70(a) (111.80(a)); in-process materials for each manufactured batch, at the points, steps or stages specified in the master manufacturing record where control is necessary to ensure identity, purity, strength and composition (111.80(b)); a subset of finished batches of each dietary supplement you manufacture, identified through a sound statistical sampling plan - or otherwise every finished batch - before releasing for distribution (111.80(c)); each unique shipment, and each unique lot within each shipment, of product you receive for packaging or labeling as a dietary supplement for distribution (111.80(d)); and each lot of packaged and labeled dietary supplements, to determine whether the packaging and labeling meet the specifications established under 111.70(g) (111.80(e)).

Reserve samples (111.83). You must collect and hold reserve samples of each lot of packaged and labeled dietary supplements that you distribute (111.83(a)). They must be held using the same container-closure system in which the product is distributed, or one providing essentially the same protective characteristics (111.83(b)(1)); be identified with the batch, lot or control number (111.83(b)(2)); and be retained for 1 year past the shelf life date, if shelf life dating is used, or for 2 years from the date of distribution of the last batch associated with the reserve sample, for use in appropriate investigations (111.83(b)(3)).

21 CFR 111.260 sets out what the batch production record must include. It begins with identification: the batch, lot or control number of the finished batch of dietary supplement, and of each lot of packaged and labeled dietary supplement from that finished batch (111.260(a)).

It must also record the identity of the equipment and processing lines used in producing the batch (111.260(b)); and the date and time of the maintenance, cleaning and sanitizing of that equipment and those processing lines, or a cross-reference to records such as individual equipment logs where that information is kept (111.260(c)).

The remaining paragraphs of the section carry the rest of the required content, including the identity and weight or measure of each component used, the dates of manufacture, the initials of the persons performing and of those verifying each controlled step, the results of any tests or examinations, and documentation of any deviation from the master manufacturing record.

The governing constraint on all of it is 111.255(c): the batch production record must accurately follow the appropriate master manufacturing record, and each step in the production of the batch must actually be performed.

Who must register (21 CFR 207.17). Unless exempt under section 510(g) of the Act or under Part 207, all manufacturers, repackers, relabelers and salvagers must register each domestic establishment that manufactures, repacks, relabels or salvages a drug, or an animal feed bearing or containing a new animal drug (207.17(a)). Private label distributors who do not themselves manufacture, repack, relabel or salvage are not required to register; FDA will accept registration or listing information from one only if it is acting as an authorized agent submitting on behalf of a registrant (207.17(b)).

When initial registration must occur (207.21). A domestic establishment must be registered no later than 5 calendar days after beginning to manufacture, repack, relabel or salvage a drug or such an animal feed there (207.21(a)). A foreign establishment must be registered before a drug or such an animal feed manufactured, repacked, relabeled or salvaged there is imported or offered for import into the United States (207.21(b)).

Renewal and updates (207.29). Registrants must review and update all registration information required under 207.25 for each establishment annually, during the period beginning October 1 and ending December 31 - the first review and update falling in that window in the year of initial registration where that registration occurred before October 1 (207.29(b)). Certain changes require an expedited update no later than 30 calendar days after the event, including closing or selling an establishment (207.29(a)).

What must be provided (207.25). The owner or operator's name, with partners or corporate officers and directors and the place of incorporation; each establishment's name, physical address and telephone numbers; all names under which it does business or is known; its FDA registration number if previously assigned; a Unique Facility Identifier under the system specified in section 510 of the Act; and all types of operations performed at each establishment.

21 CFR 211.46 sets four requirements.

Adequate ventilation shall be provided (211.46(a)).

Equipment for adequate control over air pressure, micro-organisms, dust, humidity and temperature shall be provided when appropriate for the manufacture, processing, packing or holding of a drug product (211.46(b)).

Air filtration systems, including prefilters and particulate matter air filters, shall be used when appropriate on air supplies to production areas. If air is recirculated to production areas, measures shall be taken to control recirculation of dust from production, and in areas where air contamination occurs during production there shall be adequate exhaust systems or other systems adequate to control contaminants (211.46(c)).

Air-handling systems for the manufacture, processing and packing of penicillin shall be completely separate from those for other drug products for human use (211.46(d)). That last requirement is absolute - it is not qualified by "when appropriate", unlike paragraphs (b) and (c).

21 CFR 117.40 governs equipment and utensils.

Design, materials and workmanship (117.40(a)). All plant equipment and utensils used in manufacturing, processing, packing or holding food must be so designed and of such material and workmanship as to be adequately cleanable, and adequately maintained to protect against allergen cross-contact and contamination. They must be designed, constructed and used so as to avoid adulterating food with lubricants, fuel, metal fragments, contaminated water or other contaminants, and must be installed so as to facilitate cleaning and maintenance of the equipment and adjacent spaces.

Food-contact surfaces (117.40(a)(4) through (6)). These must be corrosion-resistant when in contact with food; made of nontoxic materials and designed to withstand the environment of their intended use and the action of food and, if applicable, cleaning compounds, sanitizing agents and cleaning procedures; and maintained to protect food from allergen cross-contact and contamination from any source, including unlawful indirect food additives.

Seams (117.40(b)) on food-contact surfaces must be smoothly bonded or maintained so as to minimise accumulation of food particles, dirt and organic matter, and thus minimise the opportunity for microbial growth and allergen cross-contact.

Other equipment and systems. Equipment in food areas that does not contact food must be constructed so it can be kept clean and sanitary (117.40(c)); and holding, conveying and manufacturing systems, including gravimetric, pneumatic, closed and automated systems, must be of a design and construction that enables them to be maintained in an appropriate clean and sanitary condition (117.40(d)).

Temperature-measuring and control devices. Each freezer and cold storage compartment used for food capable of supporting microbial growth must be fitted with an indicating thermometer or temperature-measuring or recording device, installed so as to show the temperature accurately (117.40(e)); and instruments and controls used for measuring, regulating or recording temperature, pH, acidity, water activity or other conditions that control microbial growth must be accurate, precise, adequately maintained and adequate in number (117.40(f)).

Compressed air and gases (117.40(g)) mechanically introduced into food, or used to clean food-contact surfaces or equipment, must be treated so that food is not contaminated with unlawful indirect food additives.

You are subject to 21 CFR Part 111 if you manufacture, package, label or hold a dietary supplement (111.1(a)). That expressly includes a dietary supplement you manufacture but that is packaged or labeled by another person (111.1(a)(1)), and a dietary supplement imported or offered for import in any State or territory of the United States, the District of Columbia or the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico (111.1(a)(2)).

The exception (111.1(b)). The requirements pertaining to holding dietary supplements do not apply to you if you are holding them at a retail establishment for the sole purpose of direct retail sale to individual consumers. A retail establishment does not include a warehouse or other storage facility for a retailer.

Two points worth keeping. The carve-out is narrow in two ways: it reaches only the holding requirements, not the manufacturing, packaging or labeling requirements; and it turns on the premises, so a retailer's warehouse is still within the part.

21 CFR 211.68 sets three requirements.

Calibration and checks (211.68(a)). Automatic, mechanical or electronic equipment, including computers or related systems, that will perform a function satisfactorily may be used in the manufacture, processing, packing and holding of a drug product. Where such equipment is used, it must be routinely calibrated, inspected or checked according to a written program designed to assure proper performance, and written records of those calibration checks and inspections must be maintained.

Controls over computer systems (211.68(b)). Appropriate controls must be exercised over computer or related systems to assure that changes in master production and control records, or other records, are instituted only by authorized personnel. Input to and output from the computer or related system of formulas or other records or data must be checked for accuracy, and a backup file of data entered into the computer or related system must be maintained, with hard copy or alternative systems such as duplicates, tapes or microfilm.

Substitution for the second-person check (211.68(c)). Automated equipment used for operations addressed by 211.101(c) or (d), 211.103, 211.182 or 211.188(b)(11) can satisfy the requirements in those sections relating to performance of an operation by one person and checking by another, if the equipment meets the conditions the paragraph states. So automation can replace the double-check, but only for those enumerated operations and on those conditions.

Who this applies to. 21 CFR 117.206 sets modified requirements for a facility solely engaged in the storage of unexposed packaged food. They are triggered where such a facility stores refrigerated packaged food that requires time/temperature control to significantly minimize or prevent the growth of, or toxin production by, pathogens (117.206(a)).

What the facility must do (117.206(a)(1) through (4)). Establish and implement temperature controls adequate to significantly minimize or prevent that growth or toxin production. Monitor those controls with adequate frequency to provide assurance that they are consistently performed. Where there is a loss of temperature control that may impact the safety of the food, take appropriate corrective actions to correct the problem and reduce the likelihood of recurrence, evaluate all affected food for safety, and prevent the food from entering commerce if you cannot ensure it is not adulterated under section 402 of the Act. And verify that temperature controls are consistently implemented, by calibrating temperature monitoring and recording devices or checking them for accuracy, and reviewing the records of calibration within a reasonable time after they are created.

Records. The section requires records of the monitoring, of any corrective actions and of the verification activities, kept in accordance with the recordkeeping requirements of the part.

Note the limit on scope: these are modified requirements available only to a facility solely engaged in storing unexposed packaged food, and they attach only to the refrigerated packaged food needing time/temperature control - not to shelf-stable packaged food.

The label of a food in packaged form must specify conspicuously the name and place of business of the manufacturer, packer or distributor (21 CFR 101.5(a)).

The name. For a corporation, the requirement is satisfied only by the actual corporate name, which may be preceded or followed by the name of the particular division (101.5(b)).

The qualifying phrase. Where the food is not manufactured by the person whose name appears on the label, the name must be qualified by a phrase revealing that person's connection with the food - such as "Manufactured for ______", "Distributed by ______", or any other wording that expresses the facts (101.5(c)).

The place of business (101.5(d)). The statement must include the street address, city, State and ZIP code. The street address may be omitted if it is shown in a current city directory or telephone directory. The ZIP code requirement applies only to consumer commodity labels.

Principal place of business (101.5(e)). If a person manufactures, packs or distributes the food at a place other than the principal place of business, the label may state the principal place of business instead of the actual place, unless that statement would be misleading.

Hazard analysis (21 CFR 120.7). Each processor must develop, or have developed for it, a written hazard analysis to determine whether there are food hazards reasonably likely to occur for each type of juice it processes, and to identify the control measures it can apply to control them (120.7(a)). The analysis includes identification of food hazards (120.7(a)(1)); review of the current process to determine whether modifications are necessary (120.7(a)(4)); and identification of critical control points (120.7(a)(5)). Decomposition must be considered where a food hazard has been associated with it (120.7(c)(5)).

HACCP plan (120.8). A processor must have and implement a written HACCP plan whenever the hazard analysis reveals one or more food hazards reasonably likely to occur during processing, and the plan must be developed by an individual trained as the paragraph requires (120.8(a)). It must cover each location where the processor processes juice and each type of juice processed, though types or production methods may be grouped where the hazards, critical control points, critical limits and required procedures are identical (120.8(a)(1), (2)).

Plan contents (120.8(b)). At a minimum the plan must list the critical control points for each identified hazard reasonably likely to occur, distinguishing those designed to control hazards that could be introduced inside the processing plant environment from those introduced outside it, including before, during and after harvest (120.8(b)(2)); list the critical limits to be met at each critical control point (120.8(b)(3)); list the monitoring procedures and the frequency with which they are to be performed to ensure compliance with those limits (120.8(b)(4)); include any corrective action plans developed under 120.10(a) to be followed on deviation from a critical limit (120.8(b)(5)); and provide for a recordkeeping system documenting the monitoring in accordance with 120.12, with records containing the actual values and observations obtained (120.8(b)(7)).

21 CFR 211.22 sets four responsibilities.

Approval authority (211.22(a)). There must be a quality control unit with the responsibility and authority to approve or reject all components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, packaging material, labeling and drug products, and the authority to review production records to assure that no errors have occurred or, if errors have occurred, that they have been fully investigated.

Laboratory facilities (211.22(b)). Adequate laboratory facilities for the testing and approval, or rejection, of components, drug product containers, closures, packaging materials, in-process materials and drug products must be available to the quality control unit.

Procedures and specifications (211.22(c)). The quality control unit is responsible for approving or rejecting all procedures or specifications impacting on the identity, strength, quality and purity of the drug product.

Written procedures (211.22(d)). The responsibilities and procedures applicable to the quality control unit must be in writing, and those written procedures must be followed.

The pattern is that the unit's authority is defined by what it may reject, and that authority has to be documented rather than merely organisational.

21 CFR 111.70 requires several distinct sets of specifications.

Controlled points (111.70(a)). A specification for any point, step or stage in the manufacturing process where control is necessary to ensure the quality of the dietary supplement and that it is packaged and labeled as specified in the master manufacturing record.

Components (111.70(b)). Component specifications for each component used, including limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate, or may lead to adulteration of, the finished batch (111.70(b)(3)).

In-process (111.70(c)). In-process specifications for any point, step or stage in the master manufacturing record where control is necessary to help ensure that the specifications for identity, purity, strength and composition are met, and as necessary for contamination limits (111.70(c)(1)); with adequate documentation of the basis for why meeting the in-process specifications, in combination with the component specifications, will help ensure that result (111.70(c)(2)).

Labels and packaging (111.70(d)). Specifications for dietary supplement labels and for packaging that may come in contact with dietary supplements, which must be safe and suitable for its intended use.

Finished batch (111.70(e)). Product specifications for the identity, purity, strength and composition of the finished batch, and for limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate or lead to adulteration.

Product received for packaging or labeling (111.70(f)). Where you receive a product from a supplier for packaging or labeling as a dietary supplement for distribution, specifications providing sufficient assurance that the product is adequately identified and consistent with your purchase order.

Finished packaged and labeled product (111.70(g)). Specifications for the packaging and labeling of the finished packaged and labeled dietary supplement, including specifications ensuring that you used the specified packaging and applied the specified label.

To obtain a biologics license under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act for any biological product, the manufacturer must submit an application to the Director of CBER or the Director of CDER, on the forms prescribed, and must submit data derived from nonclinical laboratory and clinical studies demonstrating that the manufactured product meets prescribed requirements of safety, purity and potency (21 CFR 601.2(a)). The application must also include the manufacturing methods and facility information, and the labeling, that the paragraph specifies.

A streamlined route (601.2(c)(1)). For certain products - therapeutic DNA plasmid products, therapeutic synthetic peptides of 40 or fewer amino acids, monoclonal antibodies for in vivo use and therapeutic recombinant DNA-derived products - the application is submitted in accordance with 601.2(a) except that specified sections in parts 600 through 680 do not apply.

601.2(g) also restricts incorporation by reference from master files, but the paragraph that states the restriction was not supplied here beyond its heading, so its terms are not set out.

21 CFR 820.3(b) supplies the meaning. "Safety and Performance" shall have the meaning of "safety and effectiveness" in Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485, and the phrase "safety and performance" does not relieve a manufacturer from any obligation to implement controls or other measures that provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.

So the term is not a softer standard. FDA has mapped the standard's vocabulary onto its own: where the incorporated standard says "safety and performance", read "safety and effectiveness", which is the statutory and regulatory test.

This sits in a general rule about vocabulary. The definitions in ISO 13485 and in Clause 3 of ISO 9000 apply to the part, except as specified in 820.3(b), and do not affect the meaning of similar terms defined elsewhere in this title (820.3). And all definitions in section 201 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act apply to the regulation of quality management systems under the part and supersede the correlating terms and definitions in ISO 13485 - for example the definitions of device and labeling in section 201(h) and (m) (820.3(b)).

Two other mappings in the same paragraph work the same way: "Organization" has the meaning of "manufacturer" as defined in the part, and "Implantable medical device" has the meaning of "implant" as defined in 860.3.

Part 820 extends it by applying the standard's implantable-device traceability clause to a class of devices the standard would not itself reach.

21 CFR 820.10(d) provides that manufacturers of devices that support or sustain life, the failure of which to perform when properly used in accordance with the instructions for use provided in the labeling can be reasonably expected to result in a significant injury, must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements.

So the trigger in the regulation is functional rather than anatomical. The standard's clause is written for implantable devices; 820.10(d) carries it across to life-supporting and life-sustaining devices on the basis of the consequence of failure, whether or not the device is implanted.

That sits alongside the general traceability cross-reference, which works differently: for Clause 7.5.9.1, Traceability - General, the manufacturer must document procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of Part 821, if applicable (820.10(b)(2)). One provision routes general traceability out to Part 821; the other extends the standard's own implantable-device clause to a wider set of devices.

All three are defined in 21 CFR 7.3, and the distinction turns on two things: whether the product was marketed, and whether the violation would attract legal action.

Recall (7.3(g)) means a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that FDA considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action, for example seizure. The definition expressly excludes a market withdrawal and a stock recovery.

Market withdrawal (7.3(j)) means a firm's removal or correction of a distributed product which involves a minor violation that would not be subject to legal action by FDA, or which involves no violation at all - for example normal stock rotation practices or routine equipment adjustments and repairs. So the product has been distributed, but the defect is not one FDA would act on.

Stock recovery (7.3(k)) means a firm's removal or correction of a product that has not been marketed or that has not left the direct control of the firm - the product is on premises owned by or under the control of the firm and no portion of the lot has been released for sale or use. So the product never reached the market.

The practical consequence is that only a recall carries the Part 7 machinery: a recall receives a classification of I, II or III reflecting the relative degree of health hazard (7.3(m)), and a recall strategy addressing depth of recall, the need for public warnings and the extent of effectiveness checks (7.3(l)). A market withdrawal and a stock recovery do not.

Two sections work together.

Materials examination and control (21 CFR 211.122). There must be written procedures describing in sufficient detail the receipt, identification, storage, handling, sampling, examination and/or testing of labeling and packaging materials, and those procedures must be followed; the materials must be representatively sampled and examined or tested on receipt and before use (211.122(a)). Records must be maintained for each shipment received of each different labeling and packaging material, indicating receipt, examination or testing, and whether accepted or rejected (211.122(c)). Labels and other labeling for each different drug product, strength, dosage form or quantity of contents must be stored separately with suitable identification, with access limited to authorized personnel (211.122(d)), and obsolete and outdated labels and packaging materials must be destroyed (211.122(e)).

Gang printing (211.122(f)). The use of gang-printed labeling for different drug products, or different strengths or net contents of the same drug product, is prohibited unless the labeling from gang-printed sheets is adequately differentiated by size, shape or colour.

Cut labeling (211.122(g)). Where cut labeling is used for immediate container labels or unit or multiunit cartons, packaging and labeling operations must include one of the special control procedures the paragraph specifies - for example the use of appropriate electronic or electromechanical equipment to conduct a 100-percent examination for correct labeling during or after finishing operations (211.122(g)(2)).

Labeling issuance (211.125). Strict control must be exercised over labeling issued for use (211.125(a)); labeling issued for a batch must be carefully examined for identity and conformity to the labeling specified in the master or batch production records (211.125(b)); procedures must reconcile the quantities of labeling issued, used and returned, and must require evaluation of discrepancies outside narrow preset limits (211.125(c)); all excess labeling bearing lot or control numbers must be destroyed (211.125(d)); returned labeling must be maintained and stored so as to prevent mixups and provide proper identification (211.125(e)); and the control procedures for issuance must be written and followed (211.125(f)).

What a qualified facility is. 21 CFR 117.3 defines it by size and sales, not by any approval. Counting the sales of any subsidiary or affiliate, a qualified facility is a facility that is a very small business as defined in the part, or one to which both of the following apply: during the 3-year period preceding the applicable calendar year, the average annual monetary value of the food manufactured, processed, packed or held at the facility and sold directly to qualified end-users exceeded the average annual monetary value sold to other buyers; and the average annual monetary value of all food sold during that 3-year period was less than $500,000, adjusted for inflation.

There is no FDA approval or certification involved - the status follows from the monetary thresholds.

The exemption and what replaces it. Except as provided by subpart E, subparts C and G of the part do not apply to a qualified facility; qualified facilities are instead subject to the modified requirements in 117.201 (117.5(a)). So the facility is relieved of the hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls of subpart C and the supply-chain program of subpart G, and takes on the modified requirements - attestations and the documentation 117.201 specifies - in their place rather than a full food safety plan.

The term for that relief is defined too: a qualified facility exemption means an exemption applicable to a qualified facility under 117.5(a) (117.3).

No FDA guidance requires it, and none could. Guidance documents represent FDA's current thinking and are non-binding; they do not create requirements. So the premise of the question needs correcting before it can be answered.

The obligation comes from the regulation. 21 CFR 820.10(a) requires a manufacturer subject to the part as described by 820.1(a) to document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, and the other applicable requirements of the part. Supplier evaluation and purchasing controls are among the standard's requirements, so they reach the manufacturer through that incorporation - the standard's purchasing clauses - rather than through any guidance document.

Note what 820.10(b) does and does not do. It routes specific ISO 13485 clauses out to other Title 21 parts - unique device identification to Part 830, traceability to Part 821, complaint reporting to Part 803, advisory notices to Part 806 - but purchasing is not among those cross-references. Purchasing stays with the incorporated standard.

If you want the text of the purchasing clauses themselves, they are in ISO 13485, which is copyrighted and not reproduced in the CFR; the regulation identifies it rather than reprinting it.

Membership (21 CFR 56.107). Each IRB must have at least five members, with varying backgrounds to promote complete and adequate review of the research activities commonly conducted by the institution, and must be sufficiently qualified through the experience and expertise of its members and the diversity of the members to promote respect for its advice and counsel in safeguarding the rights and welfare of human subjects (56.107(a)). No member may participate in the IRB's initial or continuing review of any project in which the member has a conflicting interest, except to provide information requested by the IRB (56.107(e)). The section also requires at least one member whose primary concerns are in scientific areas and at least one whose primary concerns are in nonscientific areas, and at least one member not otherwise affiliated with the institution.

Criteria for approval (56.111(a)). To approve research, the IRB must determine that all of the following are satisfied: risks to subjects are minimized, by using procedures consistent with sound research design that do not unnecessarily expose subjects to risk and, where appropriate, by using procedures already being performed for diagnostic or treatment purposes (56.111(a)(1)); risks are reasonable in relation to anticipated benefits; selection of subjects is equitable, taking account of the purposes and setting of the research and being particularly cognizant of the special problems of research involving vulnerable populations (56.111(a)(3)); informed consent will be sought from each prospective subject or the subject's legally authorized representative in accordance with Part 50 (56.111(a)(4)) and appropriately documented in accordance with 50.27 (56.111(a)(5)); where appropriate, the research plan makes adequate provision for monitoring the data collected to ensure the safety of subjects (56.111(a)(6)); and where appropriate, there are adequate provisions to protect the privacy of subjects and maintain the confidentiality of data (56.111(a)(7)).

No to both.

No certification requirement. 21 CFR 820.10(a) requires a manufacturer subject to the part as described by 820.1(a) to document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, and the other applicable requirements of the part. The obligation is to have and document a conforming system. Nothing in the part requires the manufacturer to hold a certificate, and no paragraph of Part 820 mentions certification.

No exemption from inspection. A certificate issued by a third party is not a determination by FDA, and it does not displace the agency's inspection of the establishment. The part's own enforcement provision is framed in terms of compliance, not certification: failure to comply with any applicable requirement renders a device adulterated under section 501(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, and the device and any person responsible for the failure are subject to regulatory action (820.10(e)). For imported devices, 820.1(c) provides that a device offered for import is subject to refusal of admission under section 801(a) of the Act if it appears to be adulterated.

So a certificate may evidence that the underlying system was audited, and that work is not wasted, but the regulatory test remains whether the documented system complies with the applicable requirements of the standard and the part - judged on inspection.

The master record is the template; the batch record is the executed copy with evidence of what was actually done.

Master production and control records (21 CFR 211.186). To assure uniformity from batch to batch, master production and control records for each drug product, including each batch size, must be prepared, dated and signed - full signature, handwritten - by one person and independently checked, dated and signed by a second person (211.186(a)). They must include the name and strength of the product and a description of the dosage form; the name and weight or measure of each active ingredient per dosage unit or per unit of weight or measure, with a statement of the total weight or measure of any dosage unit; and a complete list of components designated by names or codes sufficiently specific to indicate any special quality characteristic (211.186(b)).

Batch production and control records (211.188). These must be prepared for each batch of drug product produced and must include complete information relating to the production and control of that batch. They must include an accurate reproduction of the appropriate master production or control record, checked for accuracy, dated and signed (211.188(a)); and documentation that each significant step in the manufacture, processing, packing or holding of the batch was accomplished, including the dates and the specific identification of each batch of component or in-process material used (211.188(b)).

So the distinguishing features are the two-person independent check on the master record, and the requirement that the batch record reproduce that master accurately and then evidence the actual execution of each significant step.

Three different routes to market, and the evidence here speaks directly to the middle one.

Substantial equivalence report. The first route is a report under section 905(j)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, intended to demonstrate that a new tobacco product is substantially equivalent within the meaning of section 910 - that is, a comparison against a predicate tobacco product that can be legally marketed.

Exemption from SE (21 CFR 1107.1). Under section 905(j)(3) of the Act, FDA may exempt a tobacco product from the requirements relating to demonstrating substantial equivalence where the modification would be a minor modification of a legally marketed tobacco product (1107.1(a)(1)); a report under section 905(j)(1) is not necessary to ensure that permitting the product to be marketed would be appropriate for protection of the public health (1107.1(a)(2)); and an exemption is otherwise appropriate (1107.1(a)(3)). A request may be made only by the manufacturer of a legally marketed tobacco product, and only for a minor modification to that product (1107.1(b)). It must identify the products, explain in detail why the modification is minor and why an SE report is unnecessary, and include a certification signed by a responsible official summarising the supporting evidence and the rationale for the determination that the modification does not increase the product's appeal to or use by minors, its toxicity or its addictiveness (1107.1(b)(2), (5), (6), (7)).

PMTA. The third route is a premarket tobacco product application, which does not rest on a predicate at all: it stands on its own evidence that marketing the product would be appropriate for the protection of the public health.

So the distinction is: SE compares to a predicate; an SE exemption dispenses with that comparison for a minor modification on the three 1107.1(a) conditions; a PMTA proceeds independently of any predicate.

The fixed interval. You must conduct a reanalysis of the food safety plan as a whole at least once every 3 years (21 CFR 117.170(a)).

The triggers. You must also reanalyse the plan as a whole, or the applicable portion of it: whenever a significant change in the activities conducted at your facility creates a reasonable potential for a new hazard or a significant increase in a previously identified hazard (117.170(b)(1)); whenever you become aware of new information about potential hazards associated with the food (b)(2); whenever appropriate after an unanticipated food safety problem, in accordance with 117.150(b) (b)(3); and whenever you find that a preventive control, a combination of controls, or the plan as a whole is ineffective (b)(4). FDA may also determine that a reanalysis is necessary to respond to new hazards and developments in scientific understanding (117.170(f)).

Timing. The reanalysis must be completed, and any additional preventive controls needed to address an identified hazard validated as appropriate, before any change in activities at the facility is operative (117.170(c)(1)); or, when necessary to demonstrate the control measures can be implemented as designed, within 90 calendar days after production of the applicable food first begins, or within a reasonable timeframe supported by a written justification prepared or overseen by a preventive controls qualified individual (117.170(c)(2)).

Two further duties. You must revise the written plan where such a significant change creates that potential, or document the basis for concluding that no revisions are needed (117.170(d)); and a preventive controls qualified individual must perform or oversee the reanalysis (117.170(e)).

Form and content (21 CFR 117.305). Records must be kept as original records, true copies - photocopies, pictures, scanned copies, microfilm, microfiche or other accurate reproductions - or electronic records (117.305(a)); contain the actual values and observations obtained during monitoring and, as appropriate, during verification activities (b); be accurate, indelible and legible (c); be created concurrently with performance of the activity documented (d); and be as detailed as necessary to provide a history of the work performed (e).

Required elements (117.305(f)). Each record must include information adequate to identify the plant or facility, such as its name and, when necessary, its location; the date and, when appropriate, the time of the activity documented; the signature or initials of the person performing the activity; and, where appropriate, the identity of the product and the lot code, if any.

Part 11 interaction (117.305(g)). Records established or maintained to satisfy the requirements of Part 117 that meet the definition of electronic records in 11.3(b)(6) are exempt from the requirements of Part 11. Records that satisfy Part 117 but are also required under other applicable statutory provisions or regulations remain subject to Part 11.

The food safety plan specifically (117.310). The owner, operator or agent in charge of the facility must sign and date the food safety plan - on initial completion, and upon any modification.

The retention period and the rules on offsite storage and availability to FDA are set by the neighbouring sections of subpart F, which govern how long these records must be kept and how quickly they must be produced on request.

What must be reported. A manufacturer must report the information required by 21 CFR 803.52, in accordance with 803.12(a), when it receives or otherwise becomes aware of information, from any source, that reasonably suggests that a device it markets may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury (803.50(a)(1)), or has malfunctioned and that this device or a similar device it markets would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if the malfunction were to recur (803.50(a)(2)).

The 30-day report. The deadline is no later than 30 calendar days after the day the manufacturer becomes aware of a reportable death, serious injury or malfunction (803.50(a); 803.10(c)(1)).

The 5-day report (803.10(c)(2)). A manufacturer must report no later than 5 work days after becoming aware of a reportable event that requires remedial action to prevent an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to the public health (803.10(c)(2)(i)), or a reportable event for which FDA has made a written request (803.10(c)(2)(ii)).

Supplemental reports. A manufacturer must submit supplemental reports if it obtains information it did not submit in an initial report (803.10(c)(3)).

The investigation duty. The manufacturer is also responsible for conducting an investigation of each event and evaluating its cause; where it cannot submit complete information, it must provide a statement explaining why the information was incomplete and the steps taken to obtain it (803.50(b)(3)), including any information obtainable by analysis, testing or other evaluation of the device (803.50(b)(1)(iii)).

The label of a dietary supplement offered for sale must bear nutrition labeling in accordance with 21 CFR 101.36, unless an exemption is provided for the product by that section's exemptions paragraph (101.36(a)).

Serving size (101.36(b)(1)). The subheading "Serving Size" must be placed under the heading "Supplement Facts" and aligned on the left side of the nutrition label; the serving size is determined in accordance with the nutrition labelling and reference amount provisions the paragraph cross-refers to, and must be expressed using the terms it specifies. "Servings Per Container" must be placed under "Serving Size" and aligned left, except that it need not be provided where it is stated in the net quantity of contents declaration (101.36(b)(1)(ii)).

Quantitative amounts (101.36(b)(2)(ii)). The number of calories, if declared, and the quantitative amount by weight per serving of each dietary ingredient required to be listed must be presented either in a separate column aligned to the right of the column of names, or immediately following the name of the ingredient.

Ingredients without an RDI or DRV (101.36(b)(3)). Dietary ingredients for which FDA has not established RDIs or DRVs - "other dietary ingredients" - must be declared by their common or usual name when present in the supplement, in the manner 101.36(b)(3)(i) prescribes.

Proprietary blends (101.36(c)). A proprietary blend of dietary ingredients must be included in the list of other dietary ingredients and identified by the term "Proprietary Blend" or another appropriately descriptive term or fanciful name, and may be highlighted in bold type. The section also provides a sample label illustrating one method of labelling a proprietary blend (101.36(c)(4)).

The requirement. Except as provided by 21 CFR 117.405(a)(2) and (3), the receiving facility must establish and implement a risk-based supply-chain program for those raw materials and other ingredients for which it has identified a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control (117.405(a)(1)), and the program must be written (117.405(b)).

What the program must include (117.410(a)). Using approved suppliers as required by 117.420; determining appropriate supplier verification activities, including the frequency of conducting them, as required by 117.425; conducting those activities as required by 117.430 and 117.435; documenting them as required by 117.475; and, when applicable, verifying a supply-chain-applied control applied by an entity other than the receiving facility's supplier and documenting that verification, or obtaining documentation of an appropriate verification activity from another entity and reviewing and assessing it.

The standard it must meet (117.410(c)). The program must provide assurance that a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control has been significantly minimized or prevented.

The permitted activities (117.410(b)) are onsite audits, sampling and testing, review of the supplier's relevant food safety records, and other appropriate activities based on supplier performance and the risk associated with the raw material or ingredient.

How they are chosen (117.410(d)(1)). In approving suppliers and determining the appropriate activities and their frequency, you must consider the hazard analysis of the food, including the nature of the hazard controlled before receipt; supplier performance; and any other factors as appropriate and necessary, such as storage and transportation practices.

Two carve-outs. An importing receiving facility in compliance with FSVP under part 1 subpart L, holding documentation of verification activities under 1.506(e), need not conduct supplier verification for that material (117.405(a)(2)); and the subpart does not apply to food supplied for research or evaluation use on the conditions in 117.405(a)(3).
